NRI Taxation

# TDS on NRI Property Sale in India (FY 2026-27): Rates, Form 27Q & Refund Guide

Published July 1, 2026Updated October 9, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- The **buyer**, not the NRI seller, is legally responsible for deducting TDS under Section 195, with no minimum threshold, on the full sale consideration.
- TDS is 12.5% (LTCG, held over 2 years) or 30% (STCG) plus surcharge and 4% cess, computed on the entire sale value, not just the gain.
- A DTAA does not reduce this TDS. The only legitimate way to lower it is a **Form 13 lower deduction certificate** obtained before the sale.
- Buyers before Oct 1, 2026, and company/firm/LLP buyers at any time, need a TAN and must file Form 27Q. From Oct 1, 2026, resident individual/HUF buyers instead use a PAN-based Schedule E in Form 141, filed within 30 days from the end of the month of deduction; no TAN needed.
- NRI sellers who are over-deducted can claim the excess back through their ITR.

Buying property from an NRI?

We calculate the TDS, deposit it and file the return for you: Schedule E of Form 141 for individual and HUF buyers, or TAN and Form 27Q for companies, firms and LLPs. If you are the NRI seller, we also handle the capital gains and repatriation side.

[Get the TDS handled](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=nri-tax)[NRI services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory)

When an Indian resident buys property from a Non-Resident Indian, the obligation to deduct tax at source falls on the **buyer**, not the seller. Most buyers discover this only after the transaction; at which point they are already personally liable for the TDS that should have been deducted, plus interest and penalty. For the NRI seller, the same transaction usually means paying far more TDS upfront than the actual tax works out to. This guide covers both sides for FY 2026-27: the buyer's rates, TAN and filing obligations, and the NRI seller's options for cutting the TDS burden or claiming it back.

Budget 2026 Update

The Income Tax Act 2025 (effective April 1, 2026) renumbers the provisions in this guide: Section 195 is now **Section 393(2)**, Form 13 is now **Form 128**, Form 27Q is now **Form 144**, Form 16A is now **Form 131**, and Section 197 is now **Section 395**. We use both names below since search volume is still on the old terms.

**In force since October 1, 2026:** resident individual and HUF buyers no longer need a TAN to buy from an NRI. They report and pay the TDS on their PAN through Schedule E of Form 141. The rates in this guide are unchanged. The next section explains who qualifies and how the two routes differ.

## From October 1, 2026: No TAN for Individual and HUF Buyers (Form 141 Schedule E)

CBDT Notification No. 121/2026 (G.S.R. 830(E), dated September 22, 2026), the Income-tax (Fifth Amendment) Rules, 2026, came into force on October 1, 2026. It added a new **Schedule E** to Form 141 for "TDS on any consideration on transfer of any immovable property covered under section 393(2)", which is the NRI-seller provision (earlier Section 195). It gives effect to the Finance Act 2026 amendment to Section 397(1)(c) of the Income Tax Act 2025, which exempts a resident individual or HUF from the TAN requirement for this one type of deduction.

**What has not changed:** the buyer still deducts TDS, at the same rates, on the full sale consideration, and a lower deduction certificate is still the only way to bring the rate down. The notification changes how the tax is reported and paid, not how much is deducted.

| Point | Resident individual or HUF buyer (from Oct 1, 2026) | Company, firm or LLP buyer, and payments before Oct 1, 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Number used | Buyer's PAN | TAN (Form 49B application) |
| How TDS is reported | Form 141 with Schedule E, a challan-cum-statement | Challan ITNS-281, then quarterly Form 144 (earlier Form 27Q) |
| Due date | Within 30 days from the end of the month of deduction | Deposit by the 7th of the following month; return by the quarterly due date |
| Certificate to the NRI seller | Form 132 | Form 131 (earlier Form 16A) |
| TDS rate | Unchanged | Unchanged |

Schedule E asks for more than the old resident-seller form did. Keep these ready before you file:

- **Property:** address, type, agreement and registration dates, stamp duty value, and total consideration.
- **Buyer and seller:** PAN, names, the seller's residential status, and each party's share of the consideration.
- **Non-resident seller:** overseas address, and the Tax Residency Certificate and foreign tax identification number where applicable.
- **Transaction:** lump sum or instalments, amounts paid in earlier instalments, and whether the gain is long-term or short-term.
- **TDS:** amount paid, rate applied, tax deducted, and the details of any lower or nil deduction certificate.

Two cautions. First, the PAN route is only for resident individuals and HUFs; a company, firm, or LLP buying from an NRI still needs a TAN. Second, if you began paying instalments before October 1, 2026 on the TAN route, those earlier deductions stay reported on Form 144; check how the earlier payments should be shown in Schedule E before filing the first Form 141, because the published guidance on mixed cases is thin. The time limit for issuing Form 132 should also be confirmed on the e-filing portal at the time of filing.

## Why the Buyer Bears the TDS Obligation

Section 195 (now Section 393(2) under the Income Tax Act 2025) of the Income Tax Act requires any person making a payment to a non-resident that constitutes income in the non-resident's hands to deduct tax at source before remitting the amount. Property sale proceeds are capital gains income for the NRI seller. The buyer is the payer; so the TDS obligation is entirely theirs, with no minimum threshold. This contrasts with Section 194-IA (resident seller), which applies only above ₹50 lakh. With an NRI seller, every rupee of consideration is subject to TDS deduction, regardless of the sale value.

## TDS Rate Table for FY 2026-27

TDS on an NRI's property sale is computed on the full sale consideration, using the base rate for the holding period plus surcharge (based on the consideration band) plus 4% cess:

| Sale Consideration Band | Base Rate | Surcharge | Effective Rate (LTCG) | Effective Rate (STCG) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Up to ₹50 lakh | 12.5% / 30% | Nil | 13.00% | 31.20% |
| ₹50 lakh – ₹1 crore | 12.5% / 30% | 10% | 14.30% | 34.32% |
| ₹1 crore – ₹2 crore | 12.5% / 30% | 15% | 14.95% | 35.88% |
| ₹2 crore – ₹5 crore | 12.5% / 30% | 25% | 16.25% | 39.00% |
| Above ₹5 crore | 12.5% / 30% | 37% | 17.81% | 42.74% |

**LTCG (Long-Term Capital Gains)** applies when the property was held more than 2 years; 12.5% without indexation, per Finance Act 2024, for transfers after July 23, 2024. For properties acquired before that date, the NRI may opt for the lower of 20% with indexation or 12.5% without. **STCG (Short-Term Capital Gains)** applies when held 2 years or less, taxed at 30%. Remember: these rates apply to the entire sale consideration, not the profit; if an NRI sells a ₹1.5 crore property with an actual gain of ₹15 lakh, the buyer still deducts TDS on the full ₹1.5 crore.

## TDS vs Stamp Duty Value: Which Amount Matters?

[Section 195](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/section-195-tds-nri-payments-guide) TDS is deducted on the **actual sale consideration**: the amount actually paid or payable to the NRI seller; not on the stamp duty valuation used by the sub-registrar for registration purposes. This is a common point of confusion because Section 194-IA (resident sellers) and Form 26QB reference stamp duty value in certain contexts, and buyers sometimes assume the same rule carries over.

It doesn't change the buyer's deduction, but it does affect the NRI's final tax bill: under Section 50C/56(2)(x), if the stamp duty value exceeds the actual consideration by more than the permitted tolerance (currently 10%), the higher stamp duty value is deemed the sale consideration for computing the NRI's actual capital gain. That higher figure (not the amount the buyer paid) is what should go into the Form 13 computation and the eventual ITR, since the tax department will use it regardless.

## Does a DTAA Reduce TDS on NRI Property Sale?

No; and this is worth stating plainly because it's one of the most common misconceptions we hear from NRI clients in the UAE, US, and UK. Most Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements give India, as the country where the property is situated, an unrestricted right to tax gains on immovable property. Unlike interest or dividend income; where a DTAA often caps withholding at 10–15% on production of a Tax Residency Certificate and Form 10F; capital gains on Indian real estate are typically **not** reduced by treaty benefits.

In practice, this means a Tax Residency Certificate has no effect on the TDS rate for a property sale. The only legitimate route to reduce TDS below the statutory rate shown in the table above is a **Form 13 lower deduction certificate**, not a treaty claim. If your CA or the buyer suggests applying DTAA rates to a property sale TDS deduction, that advice does not hold up under Section 195 as it applies to immovable property.

## Who Counts as an "NRI Seller" for Section 195 Purposes

Section 195 applies based on the seller's **residential status for the financial year of the sale** under Section 6 of the Income Tax Act; not citizenship, and not the status the seller held when the property was originally purchased. A Person of Indian Origin (PIO) or OCI cardholder who is non-resident in the year of sale is treated the same as any other NRI seller for this purpose. Conversely, an NRI who has since returned to India and qualifies as a resident (including under the [RNOR transitional status](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/rnor-status-tax-guide-returning-nris)) in the year of sale is **not** subject to Section 195; the buyer instead follows the resident-seller process under Section 194-IA and Form 26QB. Getting this determination wrong in either direction (treating a resident as an NRI, or vice versa) leads to the wrong form being filed and the wrong TDS rate being applied.

## Multiple Buyers or Joint Ownership

When a property is jointly owned by two or more buyers, each buyer is independently liable to deduct TDS on their proportionate share of the consideration paid to the NRI seller, and each typically needs their own TAN and files their own Form 27Q for their share. Similarly, if the NRI seller co-owns the property with a resident seller, the Section 195 obligation applies only to the NRI co-owner's share of the consideration; the resident co-owner's share follows Section 194-IA instead, meaning a single sale transaction can require both a Form 27Q and a Form 26QB, filed separately for the two sellers' shares.

## How Buyers Apply for a TAN

This section covers buyers still on the TAN route: payments made before October 1, 2026, and any buyer that is a company, firm, or LLP. Resident individual and HUF buyers paying on or after October 1, 2026 can skip TAN entirely and use the PAN-based Schedule E in Form 141 instead (see the October 1, 2026 section above). For everyone else, Section 195 requires full TDS compliance rather than the simplified PAN-based Form 26QB process used for resident sellers, so the buyer must hold a Tax Deduction Account Number before deducting any tax. Skipping this step is one of the most common (and most costly) buyer mistakes.

1. **Apply on the Protean (NSDL) portal:** Submit Form 49B online, along with the buyer's PAN, address proof, and a nominal fee of about ₹65.
2. **Processing time:** TAN is typically allotted within 7 to 10 working days and delivered electronically.
3. **Apply before the transaction, not after:** TAN is a prerequisite for depositing TDS via challan and for filing Form 27Q; it cannot be backdated once payment to the NRI has already been made.
4. **One TAN, multiple deductions:** The same TAN can be reused for future Section 195 deductions if the buyer purchases from other non-residents.

See our full [TAN application guide for buyers purchasing from an NRI](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/tan-application-guide-buyer-nri-property) for the complete Form 49B walkthrough.

## Step-by-Step: Deducting, Depositing and Filing TDS

The steps below are the TAN route. A resident individual or HUF buyer deducting on or after October 1, 2026 follows a shorter path: calculate the TDS the same way (step 2), then pay and report it together on Form 141 with Schedule E within 30 days from the end of the month of deduction, and give the NRI seller Form 132.

1. **Obtain a TAN:** As above; required before any payment to the NRI seller.
2. **Calculate the TDS amount:** Apply the correct rate from the table above to the full sale consideration. If the transaction involves multiple instalments, TDS must be deducted on each instalment at the time of payment.
3. **Deposit the TDS:** Pay the deducted amount to the government via Challan ITNS-281 by the 7th of the month following deduction (by April 30 if deducted in March).
4. **File Form 27Q (now Form 144):** This is the quarterly TDS return for payments made to non-residents under Section 195. It is filed on the TRACES/e-filing portal by the standard quarterly due dates: 31 July (Q1: Apr-Jun), 31 October (Q2: Jul-Sep), 31 January (Q3: Oct-Dec), and 31 May (Q4: Jan-Mar). **Form 26QB does not apply here**: that form is exclusively for TDS under Section 194-IA on resident sellers above ₹50 lakh.
5. **Issue Form 16A (now Form 131):** Download Form 16A from TRACES within 15 days of the Form 27Q due date, and provide it to the NRI seller. The NRI needs Form 16A, not Form 16B, to claim TDS credit in their Indian ITR.

## Lower Deduction Certificate (Form 13, now Form 128): The NRI's Best Option

Since TDS is computed on the full sale price and not the net gain, NRIs whose actual taxable gain is significantly smaller than the consideration often face substantial over-deduction. The remedy is to apply for a **Lower or Nil TDS Certificate under Section 197 (now Section 395)** using Form 13 (now Form 128), before the sale is finalized.

Applications are filed online through the TRACES portal and are typically reviewed by the Assessing Officer in the **International Taxation charge** that holds jurisdiction over the NRI's PAN; not a local resident ward, which is a common source of confusion and misdirected paperwork. Documents generally required include:

- Computation of capital gains; cost of acquisition (indexed, if the pre-July 2024 option applies), cost of improvement, and expected tax payable
- Copy of the sale agreement or agreement to sell, with the agreed consideration
- Purchase deed or allotment letter evidencing the original cost of acquisition
- PAN and prior years' ITR acknowledgments, if available
- Bank account details (usually NRO) for any eventual refund

Read our full guide on the [Form 13 application process, documents, and timeline](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/form-13-lower-deduction-certificate-nri) for a step-by-step walkthrough. If the property was inherited or received as a gift rather than purchased directly, the cost of acquisition follows different carryover rules; see our guide on [capital gains for NRIs on inherited or gifted property](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/nri-capital-gains-inherited-gifted-property).

If satisfied, the AO issues a certificate authorizing deduction at a specified lower (or nil) rate. The buyer then deducts at that rate instead of the statutory rate, eliminating the need for the NRI to wait months for a large refund. Processing typically takes 4 to 8 weeks; initiate well before executing the sale agreement. Our [NRI Tax Advisory team](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory) handles Form 13 applications end-to-end.

## Worked Example: TDS on a ₹1.5 Crore Property Sale

Consider an NRI selling a property for ₹1.5 crore, held for more than 2 years (LTCG), with an actual capital gain of ₹15 lakh after deducting the cost of acquisition. The consideration falls in the ₹1 crore–₹2 crore band, so the standard TDS rate is 14.95% (12.5% + 15% surcharge + 4% cess):

|  | TDS Deducted at Sale | Actual Tax Liability | Recoverable Gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Without Form 13** | ₹22,42,500 (14.95% of ₹1.5Cr) | ~₹1,95,000 (12.5% of ₹15L + 4% cess, no surcharge at this income level) | ~₹20,47,500; refundable only by filing an Indian ITR |
| **With Form 13** | ~₹1,95,000 (AO-specified rate) | ~₹1,95,000 | Nil; no refund wait |

This ₹20+ lakh gap is exactly what a lower deduction certificate is designed to avoid. Without it, the NRI has effectively given the government an interest-bearing loan until the refund is processed.

Want to run your own numbers? Use our free [NRI Property TDS Calculator](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/tools/nri-property-tds) to estimate the TDS, surcharge, cess, and net proceeds for any sale value and holding period.

## How NRIs Can Claim a TDS Refund on Property Sale

If a lower deduction certificate wasn't obtained before the sale, the NRI recovers the excess TDS by filing an Indian income tax return (typically ITR-2, or ITR-3 if the NRI also has business income) for the year of sale; even if they have no other Indian income. The return reports the actual capital gain computation and claims credit for the TDS reflected in Form 16A.

- **Filing deadline:** 31 July for most NRIs (31 October if reporting foreign assets or if an audit applies).
- **Verification:** NRIs without an Aadhaar-linked Indian mobile number typically verify via a Digital Signature Certificate or bank-account-linked EVC rather than Aadhaar OTP.
- **Refund credit:** Refunds are credited to an Indian bank account, usually the NRO account the sale proceeds were deposited into.
- **Refund interest:** Section 244A entitles the NRI to statutory interest on the refund for the period of delay, partially offsetting the cost of the over-deduction.

Filing for a refund after the fact works, but it ties up capital for months. Applying for Form 13 before the sale (covered above) avoids the wait entirely and is the better option whenever the gap between TDS and actual liability is large. Read our full guide on [claiming a TDS refund on property sale](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/nri-tds-refund-property-sale) for the complete ITR filing and documentation process.

## Repatriating Sale Proceeds Under the New Income Tax Act 2025

The new Income Tax Act 2025 (effective April 1, 2026) replaced the earlier remittance forms. The full repatriation sequence now looks like this:

1. **Proceeds land in the NRO account:** Sale consideration from an NRI seller must first be credited to their [NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) account](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/nre-vs-nro-account-fema-repatriation-limits); it cannot be remitted directly abroad.
2. **Settle the tax position:** Ensure TDS has been correctly deducted and, where applicable, the ITR refund or Form 13 certificate has resolved any gap between TDS and actual liability.
3. **File Form 145** (replaces Form 15CA): Filed by the NRI on the Income Tax portal before initiating the bank remittance, declaring the nature of the remittance and confirming tax compliance.
4. **Obtain Form 146** (replaces Form 15CB): Issued by a Chartered Accountant certifying that taxes have been paid or TDS has been correctly deducted and deposited. Required for remittances above ₹5 lakh.
5. **Submit to the Authorised Dealer (AD) Bank:** Along with the FEMA declaration, sale deed, Form 16A, Form 145 acknowledgment, and Form 146.
6. **Repatriation limit:** Up to **USD 1 million per financial year**, cumulative across all NRO repatriations (not just this one sale), can be remitted once the AD Bank is satisfied. Amounts beyond this require specific RBI approval.

Banks typically take 5 to 10 working days to process the remittance once all documentation is in order; plan for this alongside the Form 13 and ITR timelines above, not after them. Read our full guide on [repatriating NRI property sale proceeds](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/nri-repatriation-property-sale-proceeds) for the complete Form 145/146 and USD 1 million scheme walkthrough.

## Penalties for Buyer Non-Compliance

Buyers who get this wrong don't just risk a notice; the liability is personal and immediate:

- **Assessee in default (Section 201, now Section 398):** The buyer becomes personally liable for the full TDS amount that should have been deducted, regardless of whether the NRI seller has since paid tax independently.
- **Interest (Section 201(1A)):** 1% per month for the period of non-deduction (from the date TDS was deductible to the date actually deducted), and 1.5% per month for any period where TDS was deducted but not deposited (from the date of deduction to the date of deposit).
- **Penalty (Section 271C):** Equal to the amount of tax not deducted or not deposited.
- **Prosecution (Section 276B):** Willful failure to deposit deducted TDS can attract rigorous imprisonment from 3 months to 7 years, plus a fine; rare in practice, but a real exposure for deliberate defaults.
- **Downstream friction:** A flagged PAN can complicate future property registrations and bank approvals.

## Common Mistakes That Create Buyer Liability

- Deducting TDS only on the estimated "profit" instead of the full consideration
- Missing the monthly deposit deadline or the quarterly Form 27Q filing deadline; interest accrues from the date TDS should have been deducted or deposited
- Assuming Form 26QB applies because it's the form used for resident-seller property purchases; for an NRI seller, Section 195 requires a TAN and Form 27Q, not Form 26QB
- Assuming the NRI will handle TDS; the buyer's obligation under Section 195 cannot be delegated
- Not obtaining a TAN before the transaction date
- Forgetting to issue Form 16A; without it, the NRI cannot claim TDS credit in their ITR

**Official sources:** Section 393(2) of the Income Tax Act 2025 (earlier Section 195); CBDT Notification No. 121/2026 (G.S.R. 830(E), September 22, 2026) on Form 141 Schedule E; Section 395 and Form 128 (earlier Section 197 and Form 13) for lower deduction certificates. See [e-Gazette of India](https://egazette.gov.in/), [Income Tax e-filing portal](https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the TDS rate on sale of property by NRI for FY 2026-27?

For FY 2026-27, TDS on property sold by an NRI is 12.5% (long-term, held over 2 years) or 30% (short-term, held 2 years or less), plus applicable surcharge and 4% health and education cess. Because surcharge is added on top of the base rate and cess is added on top of both, the effective TDS rate ranges from about 13% for smaller long-term sales up to roughly 42.74% for large short-term sales above ₹5 crore. The deduction is always calculated on the full sale consideration, not the profit.

### Does the buyer need TAN when buying from an NRI?

For payments made before October 1, 2026, and for buyers that are companies, firms, or LLPs at any time, yes: unlike buying from a resident seller (Section 194-IA, where the buyer files Form 26QB using just a PAN), buying from an NRI falls under Section 195 (now Section 393(2) under the Income Tax Act 2025), which requires the buyer to obtain a Tax Deduction Account Number (TAN) before deducting any tax, and to file Form 27Q (now Form 144). From October 1, 2026, resident individual and HUF buyers no longer need a TAN for this: CBDT Notification No. 121/2026 (dated September 22, 2026) added a PAN-based Schedule E to Form 141 for exactly this transaction.

### Is the TAN requirement being scrapped for NRI property sales in 2026?

Yes, for one category of buyer. CBDT Notification No. 121/2026 (G.S.R. 830(E), dated September 22, 2026) inserted a new Schedule E into Form 141 titled "TDS on any consideration on transfer of any immovable property covered under section 393(2)," giving resident individual and HUF buyers a PAN-based route effective October 1, 2026, with no TAN needed. This does not extend to buyers who are companies, firms, or LLPs, and it does not apply retroactively to payments made before October 1, 2026; both of those cases still need a TAN and Form 27Q (now Form 144) as described above.

### What is the due date for Form 141 Schedule E when buying property from an NRI?

Form 141 is a challan-cum-statement, so the tax is paid and reported together. It has to be furnished within 30 days from the end of the month in which the TDS is deducted. For example, tax deducted on a payment made in October 2026 is reported by November 30, 2026. Where the price is paid in instalments, a Form 141 is filed for each instalment on which tax is deducted, and Schedule E asks for the details of earlier instalments. This route is open only to resident individual and HUF buyers, for deductions from October 1, 2026.

### How can an NRI claim TDS refund on property sale?

An NRI claims a TDS refund by filing an Indian income tax return (ITR-2 or ITR-3) for the financial year of sale, even if they have no other Indian income. The return reports the actual capital gain, claims credit for the TDS shown in Form 16A (now Form 131), and any excess is refunded to a bank account in India, usually the NRO account. Refunds also carry statutory interest under Section 244A for the period of delay. NRIs who expect a large gap between TDS deducted and actual liability can avoid the wait entirely by applying for a Form 13 (now Form 128) lower deduction certificate before the sale closes.

### Can an NRI get TDS deducted at a lower rate on property sale in India?

Yes. An NRI seller can apply to the Assessing Officer for a Lower or Nil TDS Certificate under Section 197 (now Section 395) using Form 13 (now Form 128), before the sale is concluded. If granted, the buyer deducts at the AO-specified rate instead of the full statutory rate. This is valuable when the actual capital gain is much smaller than the gross sale consideration; for example, when the property has a high indexed cost. Form 13 typically takes 4 to 8 weeks to process, so NRIs should initiate it well before signing the sale agreement.

### What happens if the buyer fails to deduct TDS when buying property from an NRI?

The buyer becomes an assessee in default under Section 201 (now Section 398) and is personally liable to pay the full TDS amount that should have been deducted, plus interest; 1% per month for the period of non-deduction and 1.5% per month for any period where TDS was deducted but not deposited. A penalty equal to the TDS amount can also be levied under Section 271C, and willful non-deposit can attract prosecution under Section 276B. The buyer's PAN can be flagged by the Income Tax department, which may affect future property registrations and bank approvals. The NRI seller's tax obligation is separate; non-deduction by the buyer does not eliminate the NRI's liability.

### How does an NRI repatriate property sale proceeds from India in 2026?

Under the new Income Tax Act 2025 (effective April 1, 2026), the NRI must file Form 145 (which replaced Form 15CA) on the Income Tax portal before the remittance, and obtain Form 146 (which replaced Form 15CB) (a CA certificate confirming tax compliance) for remittances above ₹5 lakh. Sale proceeds first go to the NRI's NRO account. From the NRO account, up to USD 1 million per financial year can be repatriated after satisfying the Authorised Dealer Bank with tax payment confirmation, Form 145, and Form 146. FEMA compliance is required throughout.

# Form 13 Lower Deduction Certificate for NRIs: Process, Documents & Timeline

July 11, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- TDS on an NRI property sale is charged on the full sale price, not the gain, so it is often several times the real tax.
- Form 13, now Form 128 under Section 395 (earlier Section 197), asks the Assessing Officer to certify a lower or nil TDS rate based on the actual gain.
- Apply well before the sale. The buyer then deducts at the certified rate and is protected.
- Without a certificate, the excess TDS comes back only through an ITR refund after the year ends.

When an NRI sells property in India, [TDS under Section 195](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/tds-on-nri-property-sale-india) is deducted on the entire sale consideration, not the actual profit. For most NRI sellers, this means the buyer withholds far more than the real tax bill; often 5 to 10 times more. Form 13 is the mechanism that fixes this before the sale closes, instead of forcing the NRI to wait months for a refund.

Want less TDS deducted as an NRI?

We work out the tax you actually owe and apply for a lower TDS certificate (Form 128, earlier Form 13), so the buyer or payer deducts only that.

[Get a lower TDS certificate](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=nri-tax)[See NRI packages](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory#nri-lower-tds-certificate)

Budget 2026 Update

Under the Income Tax Act 2025 (effective April 1, 2026), Form 13 is renumbered **Form 128**, and the underlying provision (Section 197) is renumbered **Section 395**. The application process, documents, and jurisdictional AO described below are unchanged; only the names differ. We use both terms since search volume is still concentrated on the old names.

## What Form 13 (Now Form 128) Actually Does

Form 13 is an application under Section 197 (now Section 395) of the Income Tax Act, filed with the Assessing Officer, requesting a certificate that authorizes the buyer to deduct TDS at a lower rate (or nil) instead of the full statutory rate. The AO reviews the NRI's actual computation of capital gains and, if satisfied, issues a certificate specifying the exact rate the buyer should apply. The buyer is legally protected when deducting at the certified rate, since it comes directly from the tax department.

## Who Should Apply

Any NRI selling property where the actual capital gain is meaningfully smaller than the gross sale consideration should consider Form 13. This is especially relevant for properties held a long time, properties purchased at a low historical cost, or properties where significant improvement costs can be added to the acquisition cost. Without Form 13, the NRI recovers the excess only by filing an Indian ITR after the financial year ends and waiting for the refund cycle to complete. Our [NRI Tax Advisory services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory) cover this end-to-end, alongside ITR filing and repatriation.

## Documents Required

- Computation of capital gains; sale consideration, cost of acquisition (indexed, where the pre-July 2024 option applies), cost of improvement, and the resulting tax payable
- Copy of the sale agreement or agreement to sell, showing the agreed consideration and expected date of transfer
- Purchase deed, allotment letter, or gift/inheritance documentation evidencing the original cost and date of acquisition
- PAN card and prior years' ITR acknowledgments, where available
- Bank account details, usually the NRO account, for any future refund correspondence
- Passport and visa/residency proof establishing NRI status for the relevant financial year

## Step-by-Step Application Process

1. **Prepare the capital gains computation:** Work out the actual expected tax liability with supporting figures for cost of acquisition and improvement.
2. **File Form 13 online:** Applications are submitted through the TRACES portal (the same portal used for TDS certificates and returns), attaching the documents above.
3. **Application is routed to the jurisdictional AO:** NRI applications go to the Assessing Officer in the **International Taxation charge** covering the NRI's PAN; not a local resident ward. This is one of the most common points of confusion and delay.
4. **AO review and queries:** The AO may raise queries or request additional evidence for the computation. Responding promptly keeps the timeline on track.
5. **Certificate issued:** Once satisfied, the AO issues a certificate specifying the authorized lower (or nil) TDS rate, valid for the specific transaction and financial year.
6. **Share the certificate with the buyer:** The buyer deducts TDS at the certified rate instead of the statutory rate shown in our [TDS calculator](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/tools/nri-property-tds), and still files Form 27Q as usual.

## How Long It Takes

Processing typically takes **4 to 8 weeks** from submission to certificate issuance, though this varies with the AO's workload and how complete the initial application is. Applications with a clean computation, verifiable acquisition cost documents, and no jurisdictional errors move faster. Because of this timeline, initiate the application as soon as the sale is under serious negotiation; not after signing the agreement or receiving an advance.

## Common Reasons Applications Get Delayed

- Filing with the wrong jurisdiction; a local ward instead of the International Taxation AO handling the NRI's PAN
- Incomplete or unverifiable cost of acquisition documentation, especially for older or inherited properties
- Applying too close to the sale date, leaving no buffer for AO queries
- Mismatch between the sale agreement consideration and the figure used in the computation

If the certificate isn't obtained in time and TDS is deducted at the full statutory rate, the NRI can still recover the excess; see our guide on [claiming a TDS refund on property sale](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/nri-tds-refund-property-sale).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is Form 13 and who can apply for it?

Form 13 (now Form 128 under the Income Tax Act 2025) is the application under Section 197 (now Section 395) of the Income Tax Act for a certificate authorizing a lower or nil rate of TDS deduction. Any taxpayer expecting their actual tax liability to be lower than the statutory TDS rate can apply, but it is especially valuable for NRIs selling property, since Section 195 (now Section 393(2)) TDS is deducted on the full sale consideration rather than the actual capital gain.

### How long does Form 13 take to process for an NRI property sale?

Form 13 applications for NRI property sales typically take 4 to 8 weeks from submission to certificate issuance, depending on the completeness of documentation and the workload of the jurisdictional Assessing Officer. NRIs should apply well before signing the sale agreement, not after receiving an advance payment.

### Which Assessing Officer handles an NRI's Form 13 application?

NRI Form 13 applications are handled by the Assessing Officer in the International Taxation charge that has jurisdiction over the NRI's PAN, not a local resident ward. Filing with the wrong jurisdiction is one of the most common causes of delay.

# How NRIs Can Claim a TDS Refund on Property Sale in India

July 11, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- Without a Form 128 (earlier Form 13) certificate, an NRI recovers excess TDS on a property sale only by filing an ITR for the year of sale.
- Most NRIs file ITR-2; ITR-3 applies if there is also business or professional income in India.
- Report the actual capital gain and claim the TDS that appears in Form 26AS / AIS. If the buyer has not filed the TDS return, the credit will not show.
- The refund is paid only to a pre-validated Indian bank account.

Because [TDS on an NRI's property sale](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/tds-on-nri-property-sale-india) is deducted on the full sale consideration rather than the actual capital gain, most NRI sellers end up with far more tax withheld than they actually owe. If a Form 128 (earlier Form 13) lower deduction certificate wasn't obtained before the sale, the only way to recover the difference is by filing an Indian income tax return and claiming a refund. Here is exactly how that process works.

Selling property in India as an NRI?

We work out your capital gains, apply for the lower TDS certificate before the sale, and handle the Form 145/146 paperwork to send the money abroad.

[Book an NRI property call](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=nri-tax)[See NRI packages](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory#nri-property-sale)

## Why NRIs End Up Overpaying TDS

Section 393(2) (earlier Section 195) requires the buyer to deduct TDS on the gross sale value at the applicable rate (12.5% for long-term gains, 30% for short-term, plus surcharge and cess). If an NRI sells a property for ₹1.5 crore with an actual capital gain of ₹15 lakh, the buyer still deducts TDS on the full ₹1.5 crore; often several times the NRI's real tax liability. Recovering that gap requires either advance planning through Form 128 (earlier Form 13), or a refund claimed after the fact through an ITR.

## Step 1: Determine the Right ITR Form

Most NRIs use **ITR-2** to report capital gains, since it covers income from capital gains, house property, and other sources without requiring business income schedules. **ITR-3** applies instead if the NRI also has business or professional income in India. Filing is required for the financial year in which the sale occurred (even if the NRI has no other Indian income) because the refund can only be processed against a filed return.

## Step 2: Gather the Right Documents

- **Form 16A** (now Form 131) from the buyer, showing the TDS deducted and deposited under Form 27Q (now Form 144)
- Sale deed and purchase deed (or cost of acquisition documentation for inherited/gifted property)
- Computation of capital gains, including any cost of improvement
- Bank statements for the NRO account where refunds will be credited
- Passport and residency details confirming NRI status for the year

## Step 3: File and Verify the Return

The return must be filed by the applicable deadline; 31 July for most NRIs, or 31 October if reporting foreign assets or where an audit applies. Verification is the step many NRIs get stuck on: without an Aadhaar-linked Indian mobile number, Aadhaar OTP verification isn't available. NRIs typically verify instead using a **Digital Signature Certificate (DSC)** or an **Electronic Verification Code (EVC)** generated through a linked Indian bank account. An unverified return is treated as not filed, so this step cannot be skipped. Our [NRI Tax Advisory team](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory) handles ITR filing and e-verification for NRI clients remotely.

## Step 4: Track and Receive the Refund

Once verified and processed, refunds are credited directly to the Indian bank account specified in the return; usually the NRO account the sale proceeds were deposited into. Processing time varies with return complexity, but typically runs from a few weeks up to a few months. Importantly, **Section 244A** entitles the NRI to statutory interest on the refund amount for the period of delay, which is automatically computed and included in the refund.

## Refund Route vs Form 128 (Earlier Form 13): Which Is Better?

The refund route works, but it ties up capital for months and depends on smooth processing. The [Form 128 (earlier Form 13) lower deduction certificate](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/form-13-lower-deduction-certificate-nri) route, applied for before the sale closes, avoids this entirely by having the buyer deduct closer to the actual liability from day one. As a rule of thumb: if the gap between expected TDS and actual tax liability exceeds a few lakh rupees, and there is enough lead time before the sale, Form 128 is almost always the better option. The refund route remains the fallback when TDS has already been deducted at the full rate; for example, when a sale closes faster than expected or a certificate wasn't applied for in time.

## Common Mistakes That Delay Refunds

- Not filing an ITR at all because the NRI assumes there is no other Indian income to report
- Filing the return but forgetting to e-verify it, which leaves it legally unprocessed
- Mismatches between the TDS shown in Form 16A and the amount claimed in the return
- Providing a bank account for refund credit that is not linked to the PAN or is not an active NRO/NRE account

If the sale proceeds also need to leave India after the refund is settled, see our guide on [repatriating NRI property sale proceeds](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/nri-repatriation-property-sale-proceeds) under Form 145/146.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How does an NRI get a TDS refund after a property sale in India?

File an Indian ITR (ITR-2, or ITR-3 if there is business income) reporting the capital gain from the sale and the TDS deducted by the buyer, as shown in Form 26AS. If the TDS deducted exceeds the actual tax liability, the excess is refunded directly to the NRI's bank account after processing, along with statutory interest under Section 244A for the delay.

### Which ITR form does an NRI file to claim a TDS refund on property sale?

Most NRIs file ITR-2 to report capital gains from a property sale and claim the TDS credit. ITR-3 is required instead if the NRI also has business or professional income in India. The return must be filed even if the NRI has no other Indian income beyond this one sale.

### How long does an NRI TDS refund take to process?

Once the ITR is filed and verified, refunds are typically processed within a few weeks to a few months, depending on return complexity and whether the case is picked up for scrutiny. NRIs are entitled to statutory interest under Section 244A for the period of delay, which partially compensates for the wait.

### Can an NRI avoid the TDS refund wait entirely?

Yes. Applying for a Form 128 (earlier Form 13) lower deduction certificate before the sale closes lets the buyer deduct TDS at closer to the actual tax liability from the start, instead of over-deducting and forcing the NRI through the refund process afterward.

# TAN Application Guide for Buyers Purchasing Property from an NRI

July 11, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- **Update:** from October 1, 2026, resident individual/HUF buyers no longer need a TAN to buy from an NRI seller; they use the new PAN-based Schedule E in Form 141 instead (CBDT Notification No. 121/2026, dated September 22, 2026).
- For payments made before October 1, 2026, and for any buyer that is a company, firm, or LLP, the old rule still applies: buying from an NRI requires a **TAN**, not just a PAN; the resident-seller Form 26QB / PAN-only process does not apply.
- Where a TAN is still needed, apply as soon as the deal is seriously under negotiation; it cannot be backdated once a payment has already been made without TDS deducted.
- Missing a required TAN, or filing under the wrong mechanism, makes the buyer personally liable for the full TDS, plus 1% monthly interest and a Section 271C penalty.

Buying property from an NRI?

We calculate the TDS, deposit it and file the return for you: Schedule E of Form 141 for individual and HUF buyers, or TAN and Form 27Q for companies, firms and LLPs. If you are the NRI seller, we also handle the capital gains and repatriation side.

[Get the TDS handled](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=nri-tax)[NRI services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory)

If you are buying property from an NRI, one requirement catches most first-time buyers off guard: you need a **TAN (Tax Deduction Account Number)**, not just a PAN. This is different from buying from a resident seller, and skipping it (or discovering it too late) is the single most common mistake that creates personal TDS liability for buyers. Here is exactly how to get one.

## Is TAN Mandatory for Buying Property from an NRI?

**It depends on when you pay and who the buyer is. For payments made before October 1, 2026, and for any buyer that is a company, firm, or LLP at any time, yes: the buyer must obtain a TAN before making any payment, a PAN alone is not enough, and the resident-seller Form 26QB route does not apply. The purchase falls under Section 195 (now Section 393(2) under the Income Tax Act 2025), which makes TAN-based TDS deduction and quarterly Form 27Q (now Form 144) reporting compulsory, with no minimum transaction value.**

**From October 1, 2026, resident individual and HUF buyers are exempt from this requirement.** CBDT Notification No. 121/2026 (G.S.R. 830(E), dated September 22, 2026) inserted a new Schedule E into Form 141, specifically for "TDS on any consideration on transfer of any immovable property covered under section 393(2)." An eligible resident individual or HUF buyer can now report property details, PAN, and the TDS amount directly through this schedule using only their own PAN; no TAN application, and no Form 27Q, for that transaction.

The rest of this guide covers the TAN route below, which still applies if you are paying before October 1, 2026, or if the buyer is not a resident individual or HUF (for example, a company, LLP, or partnership firm).

The practical sequence where a TAN is still required:

1. **Apply on Form 49B** through the Protean (NSDL) portal as soon as the deal is firm. The fee is about ₹65 plus GST.
2. **TAN is allotted in roughly 7 to 10 working days.** A 14-digit acknowledgment number lets you track status.
3. **Deduct TDS at the applicable Section 195 rate** on every payment, including advances, and deposit it by the 7th of the following month via Challan ITNS-281.
4. **File Form 27Q each quarter** and issue Form 16A to the NRI seller.

Paying an NRI seller without deducting TDS makes the buyer an **assessee in default under Section 201 (now Section 398)**: personally liable for the full un-deducted tax, plus interest at 1% per month and a Section 271C penalty equal to the tax not deducted.

Update, September 25, 2026: TAN Is Being Removed for NRI-Seller Purchases Too, From Oct 1, 2026

An earlier version of this guide said the October 1, 2026 PAN-based Form 141 change applied only to resident-seller purchases. That is now out of date. CBDT Notification No. 121/2026 (G.S.R. 830(E), dated September 22, 2026) added a new **Schedule E to Form 141**, specifically for "TDS on any consideration on transfer of any immovable property covered under section 393(2)" (the NRI-seller provision). From October 1, 2026, a **resident individual or HUF** buying from an NRI can use this PAN-based schedule instead of applying for a TAN. This does not extend to buyers who are companies, firms, or LLPs, and it does not apply retroactively to payments made before October 1, 2026; both of those cases still follow the TAN process described in this guide.

## Why a TAN Was Required Here, and Who Still Needs One

When buying from a resident seller above ₹50 lakh, Section 194-IA applies, and the buyer simply files Form 26QB using their PAN; no TAN needed. When the seller is an NRI, the transaction falls under [Section 195 (now Section 393(2))](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/tds-on-nri-property-sale-india) instead, which is a full TDS obligation with no minimum threshold. Historically, Section 195 compliance required the payer to hold a TAN, deposit TDS via challan, and file the quarterly Form 27Q (now Form 144) return, with the PAN-only Form 26QB process not applying at all.

From October 1, 2026, that changes for one category of buyer: a resident individual or HUF can instead use the new Schedule E in Form 141, reporting directly against their PAN. Everyone else (companies, firms, LLPs) and anyone paying before October 1, 2026 still needs a TAN, and the rest of this section walks through that process.

## Step-by-Step TAN Application Process

1. **Get Form 49B ready:** This is the TAN application form, available online through the Protean (formerly NSDL) e-Governance portal.
2. **Fill in buyer details:** Full name, address, PAN, and category (individual, HUF, company, etc.).
3. **Submit online and pay the fee:** The application fee is nominal, around ₹65, payable online at the time of submission.
4. **Acknowledgment generated:** A 14-digit acknowledgment number is issued immediately, which can be used to track the application status.
5. **TAN allotted:** The TAN is typically issued within 7 to 10 working days and communicated electronically. A physical TAN allotment letter can also be requested.
6. **Use the TAN going forward:** Once allotted, the TAN is used to deposit TDS via Challan ITNS-281 and to file Form 27Q every quarter for this transaction; and can be reused for any future Section 195 deductions.

## Documents Needed

- PAN card of the buyer (or all buyers, if jointly purchasing)
- Address proof matching the application
- Details of the category of deductor (individual, firm, company, HUF)

The process is straightforward and does not require the NRI seller's involvement; it is entirely the buyer's responsibility and can be completed independently, ideally before the sale agreement is finalized.

## Timing: Apply Before, Not After

A TAN cannot be backdated once a payment has already been made to the NRI seller without TDS deduction. Apply for the TAN as soon as the transaction is seriously under negotiation, well before any advance or full payment is made. Buyers who make payments first and try to sort out TAN and TDS afterward risk becoming an **assessee in default under Section 201 (now Section 398)**, with interest and penalty exposure on top of the TDS itself.

## What Happens Without a TAN

If a buyer pays an NRI seller without deducting TDS because they didn't realize a TAN was required, the buyer becomes personally liable for the full TDS amount, plus interest at 1% per month for non-deduction and a penalty equal to the tax not deducted under Section 271C. Getting the TAN in place first is a small administrative step that avoids a significant personal liability later. Sellers navigating the other side of this transaction can find guidance in our [NRI Tax Advisory](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory) services.

Once the TAN is in hand, use our [NRI Property TDS Calculator](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/tools/nri-property-tds) to work out exactly how much to deduct and deposit. If the NRI seller expects their actual tax liability to be much lower than the statutory TDS, point them to our guide on the [Form 13 lower deduction certificate](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/form-13-lower-deduction-certificate-nri); it's the seller's responsibility to apply, but buyers benefit from a smoother transaction when it's in place before closing.

**Official sources:** CBDT Notification No. 121/2026 (G.S.R. 830(E), September 22, 2026) inserting Schedule E in Form 141; Section 393(2) of the Income Tax Act 2025 (earlier Section 195). ## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is TAN required for purchase of property from an NRI?

It depends on the buyer and the date. For payments made before October 1, 2026, every buyer purchasing from an NRI seller needs a TAN, regardless of transaction value, since the purchase falls under Section 195 (now Section 393(2) under the Income Tax Act 2025). From October 1, 2026, CBDT Notification No. 121/2026 (dated September 22, 2026) removes the TAN requirement specifically for resident individual and HUF buyers, who can instead report and deposit TDS using their PAN through a new Schedule E in Form 141. Buyers who are companies, firms, LLPs, or other non-individual/HUF entities still need a TAN.

### Does a buyer need TAN when buying property from an NRI?

Not anymore, if you are a resident individual or HUF buying on or after October 1, 2026. Until that date, and for company/firm/LLP buyers at any time, purchasing from an NRI falls under Section 195 (now Section 393(2) under the Income Tax Act 2025), which requires a TAN before deducting any tax and quarterly Form 27Q (now Form 144) reporting. From October 1, 2026, eligible resident individual/HUF buyers instead use the PAN-based Schedule E in Form 141, with no TAN or Form 27Q needed for that transaction.

### Is TAN being scrapped for buyers purchasing from an NRI in 2026?

Yes, but only partially. CBDT Notification No. 121/2026 (G.S.R. 830(E), dated September 22, 2026) inserted a new Schedule E into Form 141 titled "TDS on any consideration on transfer of any immovable property covered under section 393(2)," giving resident individual and HUF buyers a PAN-based route effective October 1, 2026, so they no longer need a TAN to buy from a non-resident seller. This is narrower than the earlier reporting that TAN was scrapped for NRI-seller purchases across the board: it does not extend to buyers who are companies, firms, LLPs, or other non-individual/HUF entities, and it does not apply retroactively to payments made before October 1, 2026.

### How long does it take to get a TAN?

A TAN is typically allotted within 7 to 10 working days of submitting Form 49B online through the Protean (NSDL) portal, provided the application and supporting documents are in order.

### Can a buyer reuse an existing TAN for an NRI property purchase?

Yes. If the buyer already holds a TAN from a previous transaction; for example, as an employer deducting salary TDS, or from an earlier purchase from a non-resident; the same TAN can be used again to deduct and report TDS under Section 195 for a new NRI property purchase.

### Is TAN required if I buy property from an NRI below Rs 50 lakh?

Yes. The Rs 50 lakh threshold applies only to purchases from resident sellers under Section 194-IA. A purchase from an NRI is governed by Section 195 (now Section 393(2)), which has no minimum value, so TAN and TDS obligations apply even on a small consideration.

### Can two joint buyers use one TAN for an NRI property purchase?

Each buyer who is separately liable to deduct tax needs their own TAN and must deduct their proportionate share, unless all payments are routed through a single deducting buyer named in the sale deed. Fix this structure before the first payment is made.

# Repatriating NRI Property Sale Proceeds: Form 145/146 & USD 1 Million Scheme

July 11, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- Sale proceeds must first be credited to the NRI's NRO account in India.
- Settle the tax position first: correct TDS (ideally under a Form 128 certificate) or an ITR and refund.
- File Form 145 (earlier 15CA) on the e-filing portal before the remittance; a CA certificate in Form 146 (earlier 15CB) is needed above Rs 5 lakh.
- Remittances from the NRO account are capped at USD 1 million per financial year under FEMA.

Selling the property is only half the process for an NRI. Getting the sale proceeds out of India legally requires clearing tax on the gain; through [TDS and, where applicable, an ITR refund](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/tds-on-nri-property-sale-india); and then following a specific FEMA-governed remittance process. Under the new Income Tax Act 2025, effective April 1, 2026, the forms involved changed. Here is the full sequence.

Selling property in India as an NRI?

We work out your capital gains, apply for the lower TDS certificate before the sale, and handle the Form 145/146 paperwork to send the money abroad.

[Book an NRI property call](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=nri-tax)[See NRI packages](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory#nri-property-sale)

## Step 1: Proceeds Land in the NRO Account

Sale consideration from an NRI's Indian property must first be credited to their [NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) account](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/nre-vs-nro-account-fema-repatriation-limits). It cannot be remitted directly abroad or credited to an NRE or foreign account at the time of sale. This is a FEMA requirement, not just a banking convenience; all subsequent tax certification and repatriation steps assume the funds are sitting in an NRO account.

## Step 2: Settle the Tax Position First

Before initiating any remittance, the tax position on the capital gain needs to be resolved; either through TDS already deducted at the correct rate (ideally via a [Form 13 lower deduction certificate](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/form-13-lower-deduction-certificate-nri)), or through an ITR filed and any refund settled. Attempting to repatriate before this is resolved is the most common reason remittances get held up at the bank stage.

## Step 3: File Form 145 (Replaces Form 15CA)

Form 145 is filed by the NRI on the Income Tax e-filing portal before the bank remittance is initiated. It declares the nature of the remittance and confirms the tax compliance position. This is a self-declaration step, filed directly by the NRI or their authorized representative.

## Step 4: Obtain Form 146 (Replaces Form 15CB)

For remittances above ₹5 lakh, a practicing Chartered Accountant must issue Form 146; a certificate confirming that applicable taxes have been paid or that TDS has been correctly deducted and deposited on the underlying transaction. The CA reviews the sale documentation, Form 16A (now Form 131), and the ITR or Form 13 (now Form 128) certificate before issuing this.

## Step 5: Submit to the Authorised Dealer (AD) Bank

The NRI (or their representative) submits the remittance request to the bank holding the NRO account, along with:

- FEMA declaration confirming the source and purpose of funds
- Sale deed and Form 16A (TDS certificate from the buyer)
- Form 145 acknowledgment
- Form 146 (CA certificate)

The AD Bank reviews the documentation for compliance before processing the outward remittance; this is a mandatory checkpoint, not a formality, and banks routinely query incomplete submissions. Our [NRI Tax Advisory team](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory) prepares Form 146 certificates and coordinates directly with AD Banks on behalf of NRI clients.

## Step 6: The USD 1 Million Scheme Limit

Under RBI rules, an NRI can repatriate up to **USD 1 million per financial year** from their NRO account. This limit is cumulative; it covers property sale proceeds along with any other NRO balances repatriated in the same financial year, not a separate allowance per transaction. Amounts beyond this require specific RBI approval, which is a longer and less predictable process. For sales well above this threshold, plan the remittance across financial years where possible.

## Realistic Timeline

Once Form 145, Form 146, and supporting documents are ready, banks typically take **5 to 10 working days** to process the remittance. The bottleneck is almost never the bank step itself; it's the tax settlement beforehand, particularly if a TDS refund or Form 13 certificate is still pending. Building this into the overall timeline from the day the sale agreement is signed avoids last-minute delays when the NRI actually wants the funds abroad.

## Common Issues That Delay Repatriation

- Attempting to repatriate before the ITR refund or Form 13 process is complete
- Sale proceeds credited to an NRE account instead of NRO, requiring correction before remittance can proceed
- Missing or outdated Form 16A from the buyer
- Underestimating how long the CA certification (Form 146) and AD Bank review take when documentation is incomplete

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What replaced Form 15CA and 15CB for NRI remittances in 2026?

Under the new Income Tax Act 2025, effective April 1, 2026, Form 15CA was replaced by Form 145 and Form 15CB was replaced by Form 146. Form 145 is filed by the NRI on the Income Tax portal before the remittance; Form 146 is a Chartered Accountant certificate confirming tax compliance, required for remittances above ₹5 lakh.

### How much can an NRI repatriate from property sale proceeds in a financial year?

Up to USD 1 million per financial year can be repatriated from an NRO account, covering property sale proceeds along with any other NRO balances repatriated in the same year. Amounts beyond this limit require specific approval from the Reserve Bank of India.

### Can property sale proceeds be sent directly abroad without going through an NRO account?

No. Sale proceeds from an NRI's Indian property must first be credited to their NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) account. Repatriation abroad happens as a separate, subsequent step from that NRO account, after tax compliance is established.

NRI Taxation

# Capital Gains Tax for NRIs on Inherited or Gifted Property in India

July 11, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- Inheriting property, or receiving it as a gift from a specified relative, is not taxed. Tax arises only when the NRI sells.
- The cost of acquisition and holding period carry over from the previous owner, however far back the chain goes.
- Because the original cost is often very low, the capital gain on sale can be large.
- The buyer deducts TDS on the full sale price under Section 393(2) (earlier 195); the NRI settles the actual tax through an ITR.

A large share of the property NRIs sell in India wasn't purchased by them directly; it was inherited from parents or grandparents, or received as a gift from a relative. The tax treatment on eventual sale follows a specific carryover rule that surprises many NRIs, and it directly affects how much TDS gets deducted and whether a Form 128 (earlier Form 13) certificate is worth pursuing.

Selling property in India as an NRI?

We work out your capital gains, apply for the lower TDS certificate before the sale, and handle the Form 145/146 paperwork to send the money abroad.

[Book an NRI property call](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=nri-tax)[See NRI packages](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory#nri-property-sale)

## No Tax at the Point of Inheritance or Gift

Receiving property through inheritance, or as a gift from a specified relative (parent, sibling, spouse, lineal ascendant or descendant, among others defined under Section 92 of the Income Tax Act 2025, earlier Section 56 under the 1961 Act), does not itself trigger any income tax for the NRI. There is no tax event at the point of transfer. Tax only arises later, when the NRI sells the property, and it is computed as a capital gain at that point; not before.

## Cost of Acquisition Carries Over from the Original Owner

This is the rule that catches most NRIs off guard: for inherited or gifted property, the **cost of acquisition is not the market value at the time of inheritance or gift**: it is the cost to whoever originally purchased the property, going back as far as needed through the chain of inheritance or gifts. If a grandparent bought the property in 1985 for ₹2 lakh, and it eventually passes to an NRI grandchild who sells it today for ₹2 crore, the cost of acquisition used to compute capital gains is still that original 1985 purchase price (adjusted for indexation only if the pre-July 2024 option applies to the holding period in question).

## Holding Period Also Carries Over

The holding period for determining long-term versus short-term capital gains is likewise measured from the **original owner's date of purchase**, not the date the NRI inherited or received the property. In almost all real inheritance and gift scenarios, this means the eventual sale automatically qualifies as a long-term capital gain, taxed at 12.5% rather than the 30% short-term rate; since the combined holding period across owners is typically well beyond 2 years.

## Cost of Improvement Also Counts

Any documented cost of improvement incurred by the original owner or subsequent inheritors (renovations, construction additions, structural improvements) can be added to the cost of acquisition when computing the final gain, provided it is properly documented with receipts or records. This often matters significantly for older ancestral properties that have been renovated over decades.

## TDS Still Applies in Full

None of this changes the buyer's obligation. [TDS under Section 195 (now Section 393(2) under the Income Tax Act 2025)](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/tds-on-nri-property-sale-india) is still deducted on the full current sale consideration, regardless of how low the original cost of acquisition was. In fact, because inherited property often has a very low historical cost relative to today's sale value, the gap between TDS deducted and the NRI's actual tax liability tends to be even larger than on a directly purchased property; which is exactly the scenario a [Form 13 lower deduction certificate](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/form-13-lower-deduction-certificate-nri) is designed for.

## Documentation Challenges Are the Real Risk

The practical difficulty with inherited property isn't the tax rule itself; it's proving the original cost of acquisition decades later. Common gaps include missing original purchase deeds, undocumented improvement costs, and unclear succession records where the property passed through multiple family members before reaching the NRI. Any Form 128 (earlier Form 13) application or ITR computation is only as strong as this documentation, so it is worth assembling well before a sale is finalized, not during the transaction itself. Our [NRI Tax Advisory team](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/nri-tax-advisory) regularly helps NRIs reconstruct acquisition cost documentation for ancestral property.

## Practical Steps Before Selling

- Trace and retain the original purchase deed or earliest available ownership document
- Collect any succession certificates, wills, or gift deeds establishing the chain of ownership
- Gather receipts or records for any improvement costs incurred over the years
- Get the capital gains computation done before the sale, so a Form 128 (earlier Form 13) application can be filed with enough lead time

Once the computation is ready, use our [NRI Property TDS Calculator](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/tools/nri-property-tds) to see the statutory TDS at the current sale value, and compare it against the actual expected liability.

**Official sources:** Section 49(1) (cost of the previous owner) and Section 2(42A) (holding period) of the Income-tax Act, 1961; TDS under Section 393(2) of the Income Tax Act 2025 (earlier Section 195). See [Income Tax Department (CBDT)](https://incometaxindia.gov.in/), [Income Tax e-filing portal](https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/).

### More Guides on This Topic

- [NRI Fixed Deposit Options: NRE vs NRO vs FCNR Comparison](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/nri-fixed-deposit-options-nre-vs-nro-vs-fcnr-comparison)
- [Double Taxation Relief for NRIs: Foreign Tax Credit Under Section 91](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/double-taxation-relief-for-nris-foreign-tax-credit-under-section-91)
- [NRI Selling Agricultural Land Inherited in India: Tax & FEMA Rules](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/nri-selling-agricultural-land-inherited-in-india-tax-and-fema-rules)

Check our [compliance due date calendar](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/tools/compliance-calendar) and confirm the current position on the official source: [Income Tax Department e-filing portal](https://www.incometax.gov.in), [Reserve Bank of India](https://www.rbi.org.in).

### Selling inherited or gifted property in India?

We help NRIs trace acquisition cost documentation, compute capital gains, and apply for Form 13 certificates on ancestral property sales.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is inheriting or receiving gifted property in India taxable for an NRI?

No. Inheriting property, or receiving it as a gift from a specified relative, does not itself trigger any tax for the NRI. Tax arises only later, when the NRI eventually sells the property, and is computed as capital gains at that point.

### How is the cost of acquisition calculated for inherited property?

For inherited or gifted property, the cost of acquisition is the cost to the original owner who first purchased it; not the market value at the time of inheritance or gift. The holding period is also calculated from the original owner's date of purchase, not the date of inheritance or gift.

### Does the buyer still deduct TDS when purchasing inherited property from an NRI?

Yes. TDS under Section 393(2) (earlier Section 195) applies the same way regardless of how the NRI acquired the property. Because the original cost is often very low relative to the current sale value on inherited property, the gap between TDS deducted and actual tax liability can be especially large, making a Form 128 (earlier Form 13) lower deduction certificate particularly valuable in these cases.
