# INC-20A Declaration of Commencement of Business: 180-Day Deadline, Penalty and Steps

Published November 18, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- **INC-20A** is the one-time declaration under Section 10A of the Companies Act that a company with share capital has received its subscription money. It applies to companies incorporated on or after November 2, 2018.
- File it **within 180 days** of the date of incorporation. Until it is filed, the company should not commence business or exercise borrowing powers.
- Penalty under Section 10A(2): **Rs 50,000 on the company** and **Rs 1,000 per day on each officer in default, capped at Rs 1 lakh**. Confirm current amounts at filing time.
- If no declaration is filed and the Registrar believes the company is not carrying on business, the Registrar may start action to **remove the company name** from the register.
- Proof needed: every subscriber has paid the value of shares agreed to be taken, shown by a **bank statement**, and the registered office is verified.

Starting a company in India?

We incorporate your private limited company and run its first year of ROC compliance (INC-20A, first board meeting, auditor appointment, AOC-4 and MGT-7).

[Book a free startup call](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=startups)[See the startup package](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/startups#packages)

Many founders assume that the Certificate of Incorporation means they can start trading. For a company with share capital, it does not fully do that. Section 10A of the Companies Act, 2013 bars the company from commencing business or exercising borrowing powers until a declaration is filed in Form INC-20A. If you registered your company recently and have not filed it, this is the first compliance to clear.

## Who Must File INC-20A

The requirement applies to companies having share capital that were incorporated on or after November 2, 2018. A typical private limited startup falls squarely within it. A company without share capital does not. The filing is one-time, not annual.

## The 180-Day Window

The declaration must be filed within **180 days from the date of incorporation** shown on your certificate. Count calendar days, not working days. A company incorporated on July 1, 2026 should plan to file well before the end of December 2026. Do not leave it for the last week, because the form needs a bank statement and a professional's certification.

## What You Are Declaring

The directors declare that every subscriber to the memorandum has paid the value of the shares agreed to be taken by them on the date of the declaration, and that the company has filed the verification of its registered office address. In plain terms: the money promised at incorporation has actually come into the company's bank account.

## Proof of Subscription Money

This is where most delays happen. Practically, you need:

- A **current bank account in the company's name**, opened after incorporation.
- Subscription money deposited by each subscriber, visible as a credit on the **bank statement** with the subscriber's name or a clear reference.
- A match between the amounts paid and the subscribed capital in the MoA. A shortfall means the declaration cannot honestly be made until the balance is paid in.
- Verification of the registered office, with the usual address proof such as a utility bill and a rent or ownership document.
- A director DSC, and certification by a practising CA, CS or CMA.

If the company is an NBFC or in a regulated sector, regulator approvals can also be required. For help sequencing the bank account and other early tasks, see our [post-incorporation checklist](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/post-incorporation-checklist-first-30-days).

## Penalty for Missing the Deadline

Section 10A(2) imposes a penalty of **Rs 50,000 on the company** and **Rs 1,000 for each day of continuing default on every officer in default, subject to a maximum of Rs 1 lakh**. MCA also charges additional fees for a late form filing. Section 446B gives relief to small companies, one person companies and startup companies by limiting penalties to one-half of the amount, so check whether your company qualifies. These figures are reported consistently by professional sources, but confirm the current MCA fee schedule on the day you file.

## The Bigger Risk: Strike-Off and Blocked Filings

The money penalty is not the real cost. Under Section 10A(3), if the declaration is not filed within 180 days and the Registrar has reasonable cause to believe the company is not carrying on business, the Registrar may initiate action to remove the company's name from the register. Banks and investors also flag a missing INC-20A during due diligence, and professionals report that other MCA filings can be held up until it is done. A struck-off company has to be revived through the NCLT, which is slow and costly. For the reverse process, see our guide to [strike-off and winding up](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/winding-up-strike-off-a-private-limited-company-process-and-timeline).

## Practical Steps to File

1. **Days 1 to 15:** open the company bank account and obtain a DSC for the signing director.
2. **Days 15 to 45:** subscribers transfer the full subscription amount from their own accounts. Avoid cash deposits and third-party payments.
3. **Before day 120:** collect the bank statement showing the credits, and the registered office address proof.
4. **Before day 150:** file INC-20A on the MCA V3 portal with the professional's certification.
5. Keep the SRN and acknowledgment with the statutory records, then diarise the next items in your [startup compliance calendar](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/startup-compliance-calendar-year-1-3), starting with the first auditor appointment under the [statutory audit rules](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/statutory-audit-requirements-for-private-limited-companies).

## If You Have Already Missed 180 Days

File as soon as possible rather than waiting. The form can generally still be filed after the window with the additional fee, and exposure is smaller if the default is cured quickly and the company has genuinely received the money. Do not backdate any transaction or deposit to fit the window. If your shareholders never paid the subscription money, the right course is to have them pay it in, or to reduce the capital through a proper process, not to file a declaration that is not true. Our [startup advisory](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/startups) team can review the position and tell you which route applies.

**Official sources:** Section 10A and Section 446B of the Companies Act, 2013; Form INC-20A on the MCA V3 portal. See [Ministry of Corporate Affairs](https://www.mca.gov.in/).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the due date for INC-20A?

INC-20A must be filed within 180 days of the date of incorporation under Section 10A of the Companies Act, 2013. It applies to companies with share capital incorporated on or after November 2, 2018. It is a one-time filing, not annual.

### What is the penalty for not filing INC-20A?

Section 10A(2) provides a penalty of Rs 50,000 on the company and Rs 1,000 per day on each officer in default, up to Rs 1 lakh. Additional MCA fees apply to a late form. Small companies, one person companies and startup companies may get relief under Section 446B. Confirm current figures on the MCA portal at the time of filing.

### Can my company start business without filing INC-20A?

No. Until the declaration is filed, a company covered by Section 10A should not commence business or exercise borrowing powers. Receiving the Certificate of Incorporation alone is not enough.

### Can the ROC strike off my company for not filing INC-20A?

If the declaration is not filed within 180 days and the Registrar has reasonable cause to believe the company is not carrying on business, the Registrar may initiate action to remove its name from the register. This is a power, not an automatic result.

### What proof is needed to file INC-20A?

You need a bank statement of the company showing that each subscriber has paid the value of shares agreed to be taken, verification of the registered office address, a director DSC, and certification by a practising CA, CS or CMA.

### Is INC-20A required if the company has no turnover yet?

Yes. The requirement depends on the incorporation date and share capital, not on turnover. A company with no revenue still has to file the declaration within the 180-day window.

# Delaware Franchise Tax: How to Cut a USD 85,000 Bill to USD 400 With the Assumed Par Value Method

Published November 18, 2026Updated November 18, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- Delaware's default Authorized Shares calculation charges by authorised shares and can produce a bill in the tens of thousands.
- You may use the Assumed Par Value Capital method and pay the lower of the two; the tax is USD 400 per million of assumed par value capital, minimum USD 400.
- Total tax is never below USD 175 or above USD 200,000 (USD 250,000 for Large Corporate Filers).
- Annual report and tax are due March 1; late filing costs USD 200 plus 1.5% interest per month. Annual report fee is USD 50 for non-exempt corporations.
- Delaware LLCs pay a flat annual tax on June 1 instead, with no share-based calculation.

Running a US LLC or C-Corp from India?

Our team prepares your US filings and our US partner reviews and files them, while we keep your Indian side (ITR, FEMA, transfer pricing) in step.

[Book a US compliance call](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=us-cross-border)[See US packages](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/us-cross-border#packages)

The first Delaware franchise tax notice is where many Indian founders panic. A company with 10 million authorised shares and a few thousand dollars in the bank can see a bill running into five figures, and the notice shows it as the amount due. That figure is only the default calculation. Delaware lets you use a second method, and for almost every startup it is dramatically cheaper. The numbers below are illustrative and hypothetical, so run your own through the formula or ask us to.

## Why the Default Bill Looks Terrifying

Delaware's Authorized Shares Method charges by the number of shares your charter authorises, not by how much the company is worth. Per the Delaware Division of Corporations, the tax is USD 175 for 5,000 shares or fewer, USD 250 for 5,001 to 10,000 shares, plus USD 85 for each additional 10,000 shares or portion of it, capped at USD 200,000. Startups usually authorise millions of shares so there is room for founders, ESOPs and investors. The tax grows with that number even when the company has no revenue.

## The Assumed Par Value Capital Method

The alternative method looks at your balance sheet instead. Delaware states that you use whichever method gives the lesser tax, and the total is never below USD 175 or above USD 200,000 (USD 250,000 for corporations identified as Large Corporate Filers). The Assumed Par Value Capital (APV) method works like this:

1. **Assumed par** = total gross assets divided by total issued shares, carried to six decimal places. Gross assets come from total assets on Form 1120, Schedule L.
2. Each authorised share whose par value is **below** the assumed par is valued at the assumed par. Shares whose par is higher are valued at their own par.
3. The sum of those values is the assumed par value capital.
4. The tax is USD 400 per million (or portion of a million) of assumed par value capital. Capital above USD 1,000,000 is rounded up to the next million. Below USD 1,000,000 it is prorated, but the USD 400 minimum applies.

## Worked Example (Hypothetical Numbers)

Assume a Delaware C-Corp owned by an Indian founder with 10,000,000 authorised shares at a par value of USD 0.00001, 5,000,000 shares issued, and total gross assets of USD 500,000 on Schedule L.

- **Authorized Shares Method:** USD 250 for the first 10,000 shares, plus USD 85 for each of the remaining 999 blocks of 10,000 shares = USD 250 + USD 84,915 = **USD 85,165**. This is the scary number on the notice.
- **APV method:** assumed par = 500,000 / 5,000,000 = USD 0.100000. Par of USD 0.00001 is below that, so all 10,000,000 authorised shares are valued at USD 0.10, giving assumed par value capital of USD 1,000,000. Tax = 1 million x USD 400 = **USD 400**.

Delaware's own rule is that you pay the lesser, so this company owes USD 400, plus the annual report fee (USD 50 for non-exempt domestic corporations per the Division). The difference is the whole reason the method exists. If the company raises money and gross assets jump, the assumed par rises and the APV tax rises with it, so the calculation has to be redone every year.

## What You Have to Do

- File the annual report and pay the tax online by **March 1** for the previous calendar year. Delaware's late charge is USD 200 plus 1.5% interest per month on the tax and the penalty.
- Enter the issued share count and gross assets in the online filing and choose the APV method. Do not pay the Authorized Shares figure on a notice without checking the lower alternative.
- Use total assets from the year-end balance sheet (the figure that goes on Schedule L) and keep that working paper on file. A mismatch with your US return invites questions.
- Corporations expecting franchise tax of USD 5,000 or more pay in installments through the year, which does not usually apply to a startup on the APV method.

## LLCs Are Different

This calculation is for corporations. A Delaware LLC pays a flat annual tax instead, due **June 1**. The amount has been USD 300 in recent years and a late payment carries a USD 200 penalty plus interest; confirm the current figure with the Division of Corporations when you pay. Missing it also costs the LLC its good standing. For the full LLC calendar, see our [US LLC annual compliance calendar](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/us-llc-annual-compliance-calendar-non-resident).

## Where It Fits With the Rest of Your US Compliance

A Delaware C-Corp also files its own federal return and, if it has an Indian subsidiary, Form 5471. If you are still choosing between an LLC and a C-Corp, read [US LLC vs C-Corp for Indian founders](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/us-llc-vs-c-corp-indian-founders). The franchise tax is cheap to get right and expensive to ignore, so build it into your annual calendar from the first year. Our [US cross-border advisory](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/us-cross-border) practice prepares the calculation and the filing details with a US partner who reviews and files.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why is my Delaware franchise tax bill so high?

The notice usually shows the Authorized Shares Method, which charges by the number of shares your charter authorises. A startup with millions of authorised shares can see a five-figure amount. Delaware lets you use the Assumed Par Value Capital method instead and pay whichever is lower.

### What is the minimum and maximum Delaware franchise tax?

Per the Delaware Division of Corporations, the total tax is never below USD 175 or above USD 200,000 (USD 250,000 for Large Corporate Filers). The Assumed Par Value Capital method has its own USD 400 minimum.

### How is assumed par value capital calculated?

Divide total gross assets by total issued shares to get the assumed par. Authorised shares with a lower par are valued at the assumed par; shares with a higher par are valued at their par. The tax is USD 400 per million, or part of a million, of the resulting capital.

### When is the Delaware annual report and franchise tax due, and what is the late penalty?

March 1 for the prior calendar year, filed online. A late filing attracts a USD 200 penalty plus 1.5% interest per month on the tax and the penalty. The annual report fee is USD 50 for non-exempt domestic corporations.

### Does a Delaware LLC pay franchise tax the same way?

No. A Delaware LLC pays a flat annual tax due June 1, USD 300 in recent years, with no share-based calculation. Confirm the current amount with the Division of Corporations before paying.

# LLP Registration in India (2026): Process, Cost and Timeline

Published November 18, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- **Process:** name approval (RUN-LLP), incorporation through **FiLLiP**, then the **LLP agreement filed in Form 3 within 30 days** of incorporation.
- Government fees depend on the **total contribution**. Published guides list FiLLiP at Rs 500 up to Rs 1 lakh, rising by slab, and a small Form 3 fee. Confirm in the MCA fee calculator.
- Stamp duty on the LLP agreement is a **state levy**, so get the exact amount for your state.
- You need at least two designated partners, and at least one must be resident in India.
- Choose an LLP for lighter compliance and a partner-run business; choose a private limited company if you plan ESOPs or equity funding.

An LLP is quicker to run than a company: no AGM, no board meetings, and no mandatory audit below the thresholds. But it still has a two-stage registration and a deadline many people miss. This guide covers the process, the government fees as published, and when an LLP is the better choice. For a head to head view, read our [LLP vs Private Limited comparison](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/llp-vs-private-limited-comparison-india).

## The process: RUN-LLP, FiLLiP, LLP agreement

**1. Name approval (RUN-LLP).** You reserve a name that is not identical or too similar to an existing company, LLP or trademark. A published guide puts the RUN-LLP fee at a flat Rs 200.

**2. Incorporation (FiLLiP).** The Form for Incorporation of LLP is filed with the details of at least two designated partners (at least one resident in India), the registered office, each partner's contribution and the business activity. Each designated partner needs a DSC and a DIN (or DPIN).

**3. Incorporation certificate.** On approval the ROC issues the certificate with the LLPIN. Confirm in your engagement who applies for the LLP's PAN and TAN.

**4. LLP agreement (Form 3).** The agreement between the partners must be filed within **30 days of incorporation**. The agreement is stamped as per your state and signed before filing. Missing the window means additional fees on Form 3, so do not treat the certificate as the finish line.

## Government fees, as published

Fees depend on the total contribution of the partners. These are the slabs published in current fee guides. Confirm them in the MCA fee calculator before you rely on them, because commercial guides disagree on some slab edges.

| Total contribution | FiLLiP fee | Form 3 fee |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Up to Rs 1 lakh | Rs 500 | Rs 50 |
| Rs 1 lakh to Rs 5 lakh | Rs 2,000 | Rs 100 |
| Rs 5 lakh to Rs 10 lakh | Rs 4,000 | Rs 150 |
| Above Rs 10 lakh | Rs 5,000 (per one guide) | Rs 200 up to Rs 25 lakh; higher slabs above that |

## Stamp duty on the LLP agreement

The LLP agreement is stamped under the state stamp law, so the amount depends on where the LLP is registered. In Maharashtra, guides describe duty linked to the capital contribution with a minimum, and they disagree on the upper cap, so we have not quoted a single figure. Ask for the exact stamp duty as a separate line item. Some states have an e-stamping route, which is usually faster than physical stamp paper.

## Timeline

Name approval and FiLLiP are usually the quickest part when documents are clean. Delays come from name rejections, DSC and DIN issues, and ROC queries. Plan the Form 3 filing inside the 30 day window, because it needs the signed and stamped agreement. We have not given a day count because ROC processing time varies and no official figure exists.

## When an LLP beats a private limited company

An LLP is often the better fit when the business is professional or service-led with a small group of partners, when you want lighter compliance and no mandatory audit below the thresholds, and when you do not plan to raise equity from venture investors. It also suits family and partnership businesses that want limited liability without company law formalities.

A private limited company is usually better if you plan to issue ESOPs, take venture or angel funding, or sell shares to investors. Investors and ESOP structures work through shares, which an LLP does not have. The tax treatment also differs, so look at your numbers, not just the compliance burden.

## After registration

Plan for the first year: the LLP's annual Form 11 and Form 8, the income tax return, and DIR-3 KYC for designated partners. We have set out the dates in [LLP annual compliance: Form 8 and Form 11 due dates](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/llp-annual-compliance-form-8-form-11-due-dates). If you are still deciding the structure, our [company incorporation service](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/company-incorporation) covers both routes.

**Official sources:** Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008 and the LLP Rules, 2009 (incorporation, Form 3 within 30 days of incorporation). Fee slabs are from published guides and should be confirmed in the MCA fee calculator. See [Ministry of Corporate Affairs](https://www.mca.gov.in/).

We help founders pick the right structure and handle the filings, including the LLP agreement and Form 3 inside the 30 day window.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the process to register an LLP in India?

Reserve the name through RUN-LLP, file FiLLiP with the partners, designated partner and registered office details, receive the incorporation certificate and LLPIN, then file the LLP agreement in Form 3 within 30 days of incorporation.

### What is the deadline for filing the LLP agreement?

Form 3 must be filed within 30 days of incorporation. A late filing attracts additional fees, so keep the signed and stamped agreement ready before you file FiLLiP.

### How much does LLP registration cost?

Government fees depend on total contribution. Published guides list FiLLiP at Rs 500 up to Rs 1 lakh contribution and higher by slab, plus a small Form 3 fee and state stamp duty on the agreement. Confirm the figures in the MCA fee calculator, and add your professional fee.

### How many partners does an LLP need?

At least two partners and at least two designated partners, and at least one designated partner must be a resident in India.

### Is an LLP better than a private limited company?

It depends on the plan. An LLP has lighter compliance and suits partner-run and professional businesses. A private limited company is better when you want ESOPs or equity funding, because shares exist only in a company.

### Do I need an audit for a new LLP?

Not automatically. A statutory audit is required if contribution exceeds Rs 25 lakh or turnover exceeds Rs 40 lakh. Tax audit rules under the Income Tax Act apply separately.

# India to US Flip Structure: What Indian Founders Need to Know

Published November 18, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- A flip makes your Indian company a subsidiary of a new Delaware C-Corp, with founders and investors holding the US shares.
- Founders swap Indian shares for Delaware shares. FEMA covers it under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022 and the Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019 (Rule 9A on swaps added in 2024).
- The swap is a transfer for Indian capital gains tax. Exemptions are conditional, so get a written tax opinion before signing. Flipping early keeps the gain small.
- Reporting follows: overseas investment reporting for founders, FC-GPR (30 days from allotment) or FC-TRS for the Indian company, and the annual FLA return.
- Some points, such as how the round-tripping limits apply to resident individuals, are not settled. Take a legal opinion.

Choosing a structure across India, the US or the UAE?

We work out the FEMA route, the tax on each flow and the filings for every entity before any money or shares move, then run the yearly compliance in each country. Start with a free 15-minute call.

[Book a free structuring call](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=us-cross-border)[US cross-border services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/us-cross-border)

A flip means moving the top of your company from India to the US. The Indian company you built becomes a subsidiary of a new Delaware C-Corp, and you and your investors hold shares in the Delaware parent instead. It is one of the first things a US investor raises with an Indian founder, and the way it is done decides how much Indian tax and RBI paperwork you carry for years.

## Why US VCs and Accelerators Ask for It

US funds and accelerators such as Y Combinator are set up to invest in Delaware C-Corps with standard documents (SAFEs, preferred stock, a familiar cap table). Many US funds also cannot or prefer not to hold shares in an Indian company directly. A Delaware parent also gives a cleaner path to a US exit. The cost is that the flip is a taxable-looking event if done late, so the usual advice is to do it early, when the Indian company is worth little and the gain is small. Read [US LLC vs C-Corp for Indian Founders](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/us-llc-vs-c-corp-indian-founders) first if you have not yet chosen the entity type.

## The Structure

Before: founders and investors hold shares in the Indian private limited company. After: founders and investors hold shares in a Delaware C-Corp, and the Delaware C-Corp holds the Indian company (usually 100%, with a nominee holding one share to meet the two-member minimum). Operations, employees and often the engineering team stay in India. The US entity signs customer contracts, raises money and holds IP, and the Indian entity provides services to it. That services relationship is a related-party transaction, covered in [our guide to the Indian subsidiary of a US C-Corp](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/indian-subsidiary-of-us-c-corp-setup-compliance).

If the founders themselves will hold the Delaware shares while it owns the Indian company, FEMA's limits on resident individuals come into play. Many founders hold through an Indian LLP instead; see [the startup triangle structure: LLP, US C-Corp and Indian Pvt Ltd](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/startup-triangle-structure-llp-us-c-corp-indian-subsidiary).

## How the Share Swap Works Under FEMA

In the common route, each Indian-resident founder transfers their Indian shares to the Delaware company and receives Delaware shares in return, at a swap ratio fixed on valuation. Two FEMA regimes sit on top of this:

- **Founders acquiring Delaware shares (outbound):** for a resident individual this is overseas investment under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022. The 2022 Rules recognise acquisition by swap of securities as a permitted mode. Practitioner commentary notes the rules do not spell out every detail of how a swap works, and a resident individual's overseas investment carries its own conditions.
- **Delaware company acquiring Indian shares (inbound):** this falls under the Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019. A 2024 amendment added Rule 9A, which expressly deals with swaps of an Indian company's equity against a foreign company's equity.

Because the Indian company ends up owned by a foreign company that is owned by Indian residents, the structure also touches the round-tripping restrictions in the overseas investment framework. This is the least settled part of the flip. Advisers differ on how the permissions fit together for resident individuals, so a written legal opinion on the exact route is part of a proper flip, not an optional extra. We have not found an official statement that settles it for every fact pattern.

## Valuation

The swap ratio needs a defensible valuation of the Indian company, normally by a SEBI-registered merchant banker or a registered valuer, using accepted methods such as discounted cash flow or net asset value. The same valuation feeds the FEMA pricing check, the Indian tax computation and the Delaware share issue. For a pre-revenue company the numbers are small, which is exactly why early flips are cheaper.

## Indian Tax on the Swap

Exchanging Indian shares for foreign shares is a transfer for capital gains purposes. The gain is generally the fair value of the Delaware shares received less the cost of the Indian shares, taxed as long-term or short-term depending on how long you held them. Exemptions for transfers in a merger or restructuring exist in the Act, but they are conditional and tied to Indian companies, so they do not automatically cover an outbound flip. Whether any exemption fits your facts is a question for a written tax opinion before you sign. If the cost of your shares is close to their value, the tax can be small or nil, which again favours flipping early.

The Income Tax Act, 2025 applies from April 1, 2026 and has renumbered the capital gains and exemption sections. Confirm the exact current section references before relying on older numbering. The general anti-avoidance rules can also apply if the structure has no commercial reason beyond tax.

## Typical Sequence

- Pre-flip assessment: tax opinion, FEMA route, investor term sheet.
- Incorporate the Delaware C-Corp and get an EIN (see [Delaware incorporation, EIN and ITIN](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/delaware-wyoming-incorporation-ein-itin-guide)).
- Independent valuation and swap ratio.
- Board and shareholder approvals in both companies; share swap agreement.
- Overseas investment reporting for the founders and inbound reporting for the Indian company (below).
- Assign or license IP and move customer contracts to the US entity.
- Update ROC records and the Indian company's registers.

Practitioners usually quote a few weeks to a few months end to end, mostly depending on valuation and approvals. We have not seen an official timeline.

## RBI and FEMA Reporting After the Flip

- **Overseas investment reporting:** founders who hold the Delaware shares report the overseas investment through their authorised dealer bank and then file annual performance reporting as the Overseas Investment Rules require.
- **FC-GPR or FC-TRS:** the Indian company reports foreign ownership. A fresh issue to the Delaware parent is reported on FC-GPR within 30 days of allotment, and a transfer of existing shares to it is reported on FC-TRS. See [FEMA compliance for foreign investment](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/fema-compliance-foreign-investment-startups) and [our ODI guide](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/odi-overseas-direct-investment-guide-india).
- **FLA return:** the Indian company files the annual return on foreign liabilities and assets once it has foreign investment.

A late filing is regularised through the RBI late submission fee instead of the old compounding route.

## Reverse Flip and Alternatives

A reverse flip brings the holding company back to India. The 2024 Rule 9A amendment has made it more practical than it was, but it is a separate transaction with its own tax cost, so do not treat a flip as easily reversible. Founders who do not want to crystallise a swap sometimes build the US entity beside the Indian one and move new business there. Whether that works depends on your investors and your IP. See [our startup advisory](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/startups) for the broader compliance picture and [our US cross-border services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/us-cross-border).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a flip structure for an Indian startup?

A flip makes your Indian company a subsidiary of a new Delaware C-Corp. Founders and investors swap their Indian shares for Delaware shares, so the cap table sits in the US while operations stay in India.

### Why do US investors ask Indian founders to flip?

US funds and accelerators are set up for Delaware C-Corps with standard documents and a familiar exit path, and many cannot hold Indian shares directly. The request is common but not universal, so ask the investor whether it is a condition before you flip.

### Is a flip taxable in India?

The share swap is a transfer, so capital gains tax can arise on the difference between the value of the Delaware shares received and the cost of your Indian shares. Exemptions are conditional and may not fit an outbound flip, so get a written tax opinion first. Doing it early, when value is low, keeps the gain small.

### Which FEMA rules govern the swap?

Founders acquiring Delaware shares fall under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022, which recognise swap of securities as a permitted mode. The Indian company being acquired by a foreign parent falls under the Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019, including Rule 9A on share swaps added in 2024. How the two fit together for resident individuals is not fully settled, so take a legal opinion.

### What RBI reporting follows a flip?

Founders report their overseas investment through their bank and file annual performance reports. The Indian company reports foreign ownership on FC-GPR (new issue, within 30 days of allotment) or FC-TRS (transfer of shares) and files the annual FLA return.

### Can a flip be reversed?

Yes, through a reverse flip, but it is its own transaction with its own tax and FEMA steps. Recent amendments have eased the FEMA side, but the tax cost can still be significant, so treat the flip as hard to undo.

# The Startup Triangle Structure: Indian LLP, US C-Corp and Indian Pvt Ltd

Published November 25, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- The triangle: founders own an **Indian LLP**, the LLP owns a **Delaware C-Corp** that US investors fund, and the C-Corp owns an **Indian Pvt Ltd** that employs the team.
- The LLP exists because of FEMA: a resident individual cannot make overseas direct investment in a foreign company that has a subsidiary under their control. A US parent of your Indian company is exactly that.
- An LLP is an "Indian entity" under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022 and can invest up to 400% of its net worth under the automatic route.
- The chain must stay within the round-tripping limit of two layers of subsidiaries. Do not add overseas subsidiaries without checking.
- You run three entities in two countries: plan the transfer pricing, dividend tax, POEM risk and three sets of annual filings before the first wire.

Choosing a structure across India, the US or the UAE?

We work out the FEMA route, the tax on each flow and the filings for every entity before any money or shares move, then run the yearly compliance in each country. Start with a free 15-minute call.

[Book a free structuring call](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=us-cross-border)[US cross-border services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/us-cross-border)

If you are building in Bangalore or Mumbai and a US fund or accelerator wants a Delaware C-Corp, you quickly hit a question most flip guides skip: who actually holds the US shares? The founders live in India, the team is in India, and FEMA limits how a resident individual can own a foreign company that in turn owns an Indian company. The triangle structure is the common answer. This guide explains what it is, why the LLP is there, and what it costs to run.

## What Does the Triangle Look Like?

**Founders**
Resident in India, partners in the LLP

↓ capital contribution

**Indian LLP**
Founders' holding vehicle; makes the overseas direct investment

↓ ODI (Overseas Investment Rules, 2022)

**US C-Corp (Delaware)**
Raises from US investors, holds IP and signs US customers

↓ FDI (Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019)

**Indian Pvt Ltd**
Employs the team in India and bills the US parent for services

The name comes from the loop: value goes out of India through the LLP and comes back into India through the Pvt Ltd. Each entity has one job, which is what makes the structure workable for investors and defensible to regulators.

## Why Can't Founders Hold the US Shares Themselves?

Under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022, a resident individual can make overseas direct investment only in an **operating** foreign entity that is **not engaged in financial services** and that has **no subsidiary or step-down subsidiary where the individual has control**. Founders control their startup, and the Delaware C-Corp in this structure owns the Indian Pvt Ltd. That combination generally rules out founders holding the C-Corp directly.

An Indian entity is not subject to that individual-only condition. The rules define Indian entity to include a company, a body corporate, a registered partnership firm and an LLP formed under the LLP Act, 2008. That is why the founders put an LLP between themselves and the US company. Individual overseas investment also sits within the US$250,000 a year LRS limit, which is small once a company starts raising.

If your US company will never own an Indian subsidiary, for example because the India team works through a contractor, the individual route may still be open. Our [ODI guide](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/odi-overseas-direct-investment-guide-india) covers the individual and entity routes side by side.

## Why an LLP and Not a Second Private Limited Company?

- **Lighter compliance:** an LLP has no board meetings or AGM and files Form 8 and Form 11 each year. See [LLP Form 8 and Form 11 due dates](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/llp-annual-compliance-form-8-form-11-due-dates).
- **Tax on the way out:** an LLP is taxed as a firm, and a partner's share of profit that has already been taxed in the LLP is not taxed again in the partner's hands. A company paying dividends to founders adds a second layer of tax.
- **Founder control:** the LLP agreement sets each founder's share and decision rights, mirroring the founders' agreed split in the US company.

A private limited company can also hold the US shares, and some founders prefer it when they expect outside investors at the holding level. The choice is mainly about tax on distributions and how much compliance you want to carry. Our [LLP vs private limited comparison](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/llp-vs-private-limited-comparison-india) sets out the trade-offs.

## How Much Can the LLP Invest?

Under the automatic route, an Indian entity's total financial commitment in overseas direct investment can go up to **400% of its net worth** as on the date of its last audited balance sheet. For an LLP, net worth is the partners' capital contribution plus undistributed profits. Two practical points follow:

- Founders need to put real capital into the LLP before it invests, because the limit is measured against the LLP's own net worth.
- A newly formed LLP may not have an audited balance sheet yet. Ask your authorised dealer bank early how it will measure net worth for your first remittance, so the timing of your US round does not get stuck.

## Is This Round Tripping?

Money leaving India and coming back is the textbook concern behind round-tripping rules. The 2022 rules replaced the old near-ban with a limit: a person resident in India cannot make a financial commitment in a foreign entity that has invested, or later invests, into India if the result is a structure with **more than two layers of subsidiaries**. The test applies at the time of investment and at any time afterwards.

Practitioner commentary generally reads a plain LLP, US C-Corp and Indian Pvt Ltd chain as within the limit. The risk comes later: adding a UK or Singapore subsidiary under the US company, or a second Indian subsidiary under the first, can push you over. Keep a written layer count with your FEMA file and check it before every new entity. The general anti-avoidance rules can also apply to any structure that exists mainly for tax, so document the commercial reason: the investor's requirement for a Delaware parent.

## How Does the Indian Pvt Ltd Fit In?

The Indian company receives foreign investment from the US parent under the Non-Debt Instruments Rules, 2019. Most technology and services sectors are under the automatic route, but check your sector and any land-border investor in the cap table. The Indian company then:

- Reports the share allotment to the US parent on **FC-GPR within 30 days** and files the annual **FLA return**.
- Employs the team and usually bills the US parent a service fee, often cost plus a markup. That is an international transaction, so **transfer pricing** applies and Form 3CEB is required whatever the amount. See our [guide to the Indian subsidiary of a US C-Corp](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/indian-subsidiary-of-us-c-corp-setup-compliance).
- Runs normal Indian compliance: ROC filings, statutory audit, ITR, TDS, GST and payroll.

Employee stock options are usually granted by the US parent. The 2022 rules allow employees of an Indian subsidiary to acquire such options, and the benefit is taxed in India as salary on exercise. Plan the ESOP pool with the US counsel and the Indian payroll together; see [ESOP structuring for Indian startups](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/esop-structuring-indian-startups).

## What About Tax Across the Three Entities?

| Flow | What to plan for |
| --- | --- |
| US parent pays the Indian Pvt Ltd for services | Arm's length markup, transfer pricing documentation, Indian corporate tax on the margin |
| US C-Corp profits | US federal and state corporate tax; Form 1120 with Form 5472 because it is foreign-owned |
| Dividend from the US C-Corp to the LLP | US withholding tax reduced under the India-US DTAA (the rate depends on the type of shareholder, so confirm how the LLP is treated); taxed in India in the LLP with credit for US tax |
| LLP to founders | LLP taxed as a firm; profit share already taxed in the LLP is not taxed again for the partners |
| Exit (sale of the US company) | Gain arises in the LLP, which sold the shares; plan how proceeds reach the founders before you sign |

One more risk: if all the real decisions of the US C-Corp are taken by founders sitting in India, the US company can be treated as resident in India under the place of effective management test. Hold US board meetings properly and keep records of where decisions are taken. Our [POEM guide](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/poem-place-of-effective-management-india) explains the test. The Income Tax Act, 2025 has renumbered the relevant sections, so confirm current references before relying on older numbering.

## What Filings Does the Triangle Create Each Year?

- **Indian LLP:** Form 11 and Form 8, ITR, the ODI annual performance report through the bank, and the FLA return where it applies.
- **US C-Corp:** Form 1120 with Form 5472, Delaware franchise tax and annual report (see [the Assumed Par Value method](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/delaware-franchise-tax-assumed-par-value-method)), and state filings where you have nexus.
- **Indian Pvt Ltd:** AOC-4 and MGT-7, statutory audit, ITR with Form 3CEB, FC-GPR on each allotment, FLA return, TDS, GST and payroll.

Late FEMA reports are regularised through the RBI late submission fee, which is cheaper and simpler when caught early. Keep one compliance calendar across all three entities rather than three separate ones.

## How Do You Set It Up, Step by Step?

1. Agree the structure with your lead investor and get a written FEMA and tax view on your exact facts.
2. Incorporate the Indian LLP and bring in the founders' capital. See [LLP registration process and cost](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/llp-registration-process-cost-india-2026).
3. Incorporate the Delaware C-Corp and get its EIN (see [Delaware incorporation, EIN and ITIN](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/delaware-wyoming-incorporation-ein-itin-guide)).
4. The LLP subscribes to the C-Corp shares through its authorised dealer bank, with the ODI reporting.
5. Incorporate the Indian Pvt Ltd with the C-Corp as shareholder, or move an existing Indian company under it through a flip (see [India to US flip structure](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/india-to-us-flip-structure-guide)).
6. Sign the intercompany services agreement and IP assignment, set the transfer pricing policy, and file FC-GPR within 30 days of allotment.

## When Is the Triangle the Wrong Choice?

- **You are not raising from US investors:** an Indian Pvt Ltd on its own, with a US subsidiary for US sales if needed, is simpler and keeps an Indian IPO open.
- **You may want to list in India:** a number of well-known Indian startups have moved their holding company back to India in recent years. The 2024 fast-track merger route for a foreign holding company merging into its Indian wholly owned subsidiary has made a reverse flip more practical, but it still has a tax cost.
- **The team is tiny and early:** three entities mean three sets of filings. If a US C-Corp is only a fundraising formality, compare the cost against a later flip.

The structure is a tool, not a badge. If your investor needs a Delaware parent and your team is in India, it solves a real FEMA problem. If not, the simpler structure usually wins. See [our US cross-border services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/us-cross-border) and [startup services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/startups) for how we run all three entities together.

The most common alternative is to keep India at the top: see [Indian Pvt Ltd holding with a US or UAE subsidiary](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/indian-holding-company-us-uae-subsidiary-structure).

**Official sources:** Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022 and Regulations, 2022, and the RBI Master Direction on Overseas Investment; Foreign Exchange Management (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019; Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations) Amendment Rules, 2024. See [Reserve Bank of India](https://www.rbi.org.in/). This guide is general information, not advice on your facts.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the triangle structure for Indian startups?

The founders form an Indian LLP. The LLP invests in a Delaware C-Corp, which is the company US investors fund. The C-Corp then owns an Indian private limited company that employs the team in India. Money and shares move in a loop: India to the US through the LLP, and back to India as foreign investment in the Pvt Ltd.

### Why not hold the US C-Corp shares personally?

Under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022, a resident individual can make overseas direct investment only in an operating foreign company that is not in financial services and that has no subsidiary or step-down subsidiary under the individual's control. A Delaware C-Corp that owns your Indian Pvt Ltd has exactly such a subsidiary, so founders who control it usually cannot hold it directly. An Indian entity such as an LLP is not subject to that restriction.

### Can an LLP make overseas direct investment?

Yes. The Overseas Investment Rules treat an LLP formed under the LLP Act, 2008 as an Indian entity. An Indian entity can commit up to 400% of its net worth, as per its last audited balance sheet, under the automatic route. For an LLP, net worth is the partners' capital contribution plus undistributed profits.

### Is the triangle structure round tripping?

It is an ODI-FDI structure, which the 2022 rules allow subject to a limit: a resident cannot invest in a foreign entity that invests into India if the result is more than two layers of subsidiaries. A plain LLP, US C-Corp and Indian Pvt Ltd chain is generally read as within the limit, but adding more overseas subsidiaries can break it. Get the layer count confirmed in writing.

### How is money taxed as it moves through the triangle?

The Indian Pvt Ltd usually earns a service fee from the US parent, priced at arm's length under transfer pricing. Dividends from the US C-Corp to the LLP face US withholding tax, reduced under the India-US DTAA, and are taxed in India in the LLP's hands with credit for the US tax. The LLP itself is taxed as a firm. Model these flows before you raise.

### Do US investors accept an LLP on the cap table?

Many do, because it is a known answer to the Indian ODI rules, but some prefer founders to hold shares personally for vesting and exit reasons. Raise it with the investor and their counsel at the term sheet stage, not at closing.

### What does it cost to run the triangle every year?

Three sets of compliance: the LLP (Form 8, Form 11, ITR and ODI annual performance report), the US C-Corp (Form 1120, Form 5472, Delaware franchise tax and annual report) and the Indian Pvt Ltd (ROC filings, audit, ITR, transfer pricing report and FLA return). The cost depends on the size of each entity and which filings apply, so plan for all three from the start.

# Indian Pvt Ltd as Holding Company With a US C-Corp or UAE Subsidiary

Published November 25, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- The structure: founders own an **Indian Pvt Ltd** (the head office), which owns a **US C-Corp**, a **UAE company** or both for international operations.
- The Indian company makes the overseas direct investment, up to 400% of its net worth under the automatic route. Founders make no ODI themselves.
- Subsidiary profits are taxed abroad and taxed in India only when paid up as dividends, with foreign tax credit, provided the subsidiary is really managed abroad.
- Plan transfer pricing between India and each subsidiary, the POEM test, and the yearly ODI filings (including the Annual Performance Report by December 31).
- Best when you will raise from Indian or global investors who are happy at the Indian level, or want an Indian IPO. If US VCs insist on a Delaware parent, look at a flip instead.

Choosing a structure across India, the US or the UAE?

We work out the FEMA route, the tax on each flow and the filings for every entity before any money or shares move, then run the yearly compliance in each country. Start with a free 15-minute call.

[Book a free structuring call](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=us-cross-border)[US cross-border services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/us-cross-border)

Not every founder needs a Delaware parent. If you are building in Bangalore or Mumbai, raising from Indian funds, and selling to customers in the US or the Gulf, the simplest group often keeps India at the top: the Indian private limited company is the head office and owns the overseas companies. This guide covers how that works under FEMA, how the US and UAE subsidiaries are taxed, and what it takes to keep it compliant.

## What Does the Structure Look Like?

**Founders and investors**
Hold shares in the Indian company only

↓ equity

**Indian Pvt Ltd (head office)**
Owns the IP, employs the core team, raises capital

↓ ODI (Overseas Investment Rules, 2022)

**US C-Corp**
US customers, contracts, bank account, US hires

**UAE company**
Gulf and Middle East sales, regional team

Money flows one way at the start: out of India as investment in the subsidiaries. Later, profits come back as dividends or as fees for services the Indian company provides. Nothing comes back into India as foreign investment, which keeps round-tripping questions simple.

## Why Keep the Head Office in India?

- **No ODI for founders:** founders hold Indian shares only. The individual ODI conditions and the US$250,000 LRS limit do not apply to them, unlike a structure where founders hold a foreign parent.
- **Indian listing stays open:** an Indian company can list in India directly. A number of well-known startups have spent time and tax moving their holding company back to India; starting here avoids that.
- **Simpler ESOPs:** options are granted by the Indian company to Indian employees under Indian rules, with no foreign security involved.
- **One cap table, in India:** Indian funds, angels and DPIIT-linked benefits sit naturally at the Indian company.

The trade-off is US venture capital. Many US funds and accelerators prefer to invest in a Delaware C-Corp at the top of the group. If that is your plan, read our [India to US flip guide](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/india-to-us-flip-structure-guide) and the [LLP, US C-Corp and Pvt Ltd triangle](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/startup-triangle-structure-llp-us-c-corp-indian-subsidiary) before you choose.

## Which Structure Fits Which Founder?

| Structure | Top company | Usually suits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| India-first holding (this guide) | Indian Pvt Ltd | Indian investors, Indian IPO plans, India-built product selling abroad |
| Flip | Delaware C-Corp | US VC or accelerator funding where a Delaware parent is a condition |
| LLP triangle | Delaware C-Corp, held by founders through an Indian LLP | US funding with India-resident founders who need an Indian entity to make the ODI |

## How Does the Indian Company Invest Abroad Under FEMA?

An Indian company investing in a foreign company it controls is making overseas direct investment under the Foreign Exchange Management (Overseas Investment) Rules, 2022. In practice:

- **Automatic route:** no RBI approval is needed if the total financial commitment (equity, loans and guarantees to the subsidiary) stays within **400% of the Indian company's net worth** as per its last audited balance sheet, and the subsidiary is in a bona fide business. Commitments of US$1 billion or more in a financial year need RBI approval.
- **Through your bank:** the remittance and the ODI reporting go through your authorised dealer bank, which reports it to RBI. Do not wire money for the US or UAE company before the bank has your ODI paperwork; that is a common and avoidable FEMA breach.
- **Annual Performance Report:** the Indian company files an APR for each subsidiary through the bank, generally by **December 31** each year, based on the subsidiary's accounts. It also files the annual FLA return.
- **Late filings:** missed ODI reports are regularised through the RBI late submission fee, and banks can hold back further remittances until the backlog is cleared.

One limit to keep in mind: if the US or UAE subsidiary later invests back into India, the round-tripping rules apply and the structure must not exceed two layers of subsidiaries. Keep the overseas companies as operating companies, not channels for money coming back in. Our [ODI guide](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/odi-overseas-direct-investment-guide-india) covers the reporting in more detail.

## The US C-Corp as a Subsidiary

A US subsidiary is usually set up so US customers can contract with a US company, pay into a US bank account and deal with a US team. A Delaware C-Corp is the common choice; see [US LLC vs C-Corp](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/us-llc-vs-c-corp-indian-founders) for when an LLC can work instead.

- **US tax:** the C-Corp pays US federal corporate tax and any state tax where it does business.
- **Foreign-owned filings:** because an Indian company owns it, the C-Corp files Form 1120 with **Form 5472** reporting transactions with its Indian parent. See [Forms 5471, 5472 and 8858](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/form-5471-5472-8858-foreign-owned-us-entity).
- **Delaware:** annual franchise tax and annual report; use the [Assumed Par Value method](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/delaware-franchise-tax-assumed-par-value-method) to avoid an inflated bill.
- **Dividends to India:** under the India-US DTAA, US withholding on dividends is limited to **15%** where the Indian company holds at least 10% of the voting stock. India taxes the dividend in the parent's hands and allows credit for the US tax.

## The UAE Company as a Subsidiary

A UAE subsidiary makes sense when you have real customers, partners or staff in the Gulf. Our [honest guide to when a UAE entity makes sense](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/uae-entity-setup-when-it-makes-sense) covers the business case, and the [Dubai company registration guide](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/dubai-company-registration-guide) covers mainland versus free zone.

- **UAE corporate tax:** 0% on taxable income up to AED 375,000 and 9% above that.
- **Free zone 0%:** a qualifying free zone person can get 0% on qualifying income, but only with adequate substance in the free zone (people and core activities there), audited accounts, transfer pricing compliance and a cap on non-qualifying revenue. See [UAE corporate tax for Indian businesses](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/uae-corporate-tax-indian-impact).
- **Transfer pricing on both sides:** the UAE now expects arm's length pricing too, so the India-UAE service or distribution arrangement needs one consistent policy. See [India-UAE transfer pricing](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/india-uae-transfer-pricing-compliance).

A UAE company that has no staff or decision-making in the UAE and simply books profit earned by the Indian team is the version that goes wrong: it fails UAE substance, invites an Indian transfer pricing adjustment, and can be treated as Indian-resident under POEM.

## How Is Money Taxed Between India and the Subsidiaries?

| Flow | What to plan for |
| --- | --- |
| Indian company builds the product, subsidiary sells it | Arm's length fee or margin for the Indian company (development services, licence of IP or distribution margin), with transfer pricing documentation and Form 3CEB |
| Subsidiary profits | Taxed in the US or UAE where earned; not taxed in India while retained, provided the subsidiary is managed abroad |
| Dividend to the Indian parent | Taxed in India in the parent's hands with credit for foreign tax under the DTAA; claim the credit with the prescribed form in your Indian return |
| Loans or guarantees from the Indian parent | Count towards the ODI financial commitment limit; interest and guarantee fees need arm's length pricing |
| Exit by selling the subsidiary | Capital gains in the Indian company; ODI disinvestment reporting through the bank |

See [transfer pricing for IT services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/transfer-pricing-it-services-india) and [Form 3CEB](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/form-3ceb-transfer-pricing-audit-report) for the Indian side. The Income Tax Act, 2025 has renumbered the transfer pricing, foreign tax credit and residence sections, so confirm current references before relying on older numbering.

## What Is the POEM Risk for a Foreign Subsidiary?

A foreign company is treated as resident in India if its place of effective management, where key management and commercial decisions are in substance made, is in India. With the head office in India, this is the main tax risk of the structure: if the Indian founders take every decision for the US or UAE company from Bangalore or Mumbai, India can tax its global income.

CBDT has said the POEM test does not apply to a foreign company with turnover or gross receipts of Rs 50 crore or less in a financial year, and there is separate guidance for companies engaged in active business outside India. Above that size, give each subsidiary real local management: a local director or senior manager, board meetings held and minuted outside India, and local authority to sign contracts and hire. Our [POEM guide](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/poem-place-of-effective-management-india) explains the tests.

## What Filings Does the Group Have Each Year?

- **Indian Pvt Ltd:** AOC-4 and MGT-7, statutory audit, ITR with Form 3CEB, the APR for each subsidiary, the FLA return, TDS, GST and payroll.
- **US C-Corp:** Form 1120 with Form 5472, Delaware franchise tax and annual report, and state filings where it has nexus.
- **UAE company:** corporate tax registration and return, audited financial statements where required (including for free zone 0% status), VAT if registered, transfer pricing disclosures, and the licence renewal for its zone.

The APR depends on the subsidiaries' accounts, so close the US and UAE books early enough to meet the December 31 date in India.

## How Do You Set It Up, Step by Step?

1. Decide which markets need a local company, and whether a US, UAE or both subsidiaries make sense now.
2. Check the Indian company's audited net worth against the planned investment, loans and guarantees.
3. Pass the board resolution approving the overseas investment and fix the subsidiary's capital.
4. Incorporate the subsidiary (see [Delaware incorporation and EIN](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/delaware-wyoming-incorporation-ein-itin-guide) or the [Dubai registration guide](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/dubai-company-registration-guide)).
5. Submit the ODI paperwork to your bank and remit the capital through it.
6. Sign the intercompany agreement (services, IP licence or distribution), set the transfer pricing policy, and appoint local management.
7. Put the APR, FLA, Form 3CEB and foreign filing dates into one group compliance calendar.

## When Is This the Wrong Structure?

- **A US fund needs a Delaware parent:** converting later means a flip, with its own tax cost. Decide before the term sheet.
- **The overseas company would have no real activity:** a subsidiary with no staff, customers or local decisions adds cost and tax risk without benefit. Selling from India with an export invoice may be enough for now.
- **The Indian company has little net worth:** the 400% limit is measured against audited net worth, so a very early company may need to raise equity before it can fund a subsidiary.

For most India-built startups and services businesses expanding to the US or the Gulf, India-first is the cleanest starting point. See [our US cross-border services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/us-cross-border), [UAE tax advisory](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/uae-tax-advisory) and [startup services](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/startups) for how we run the group's compliance across all three countries.

See [Reserve Bank of India](https://www.rbi.org.in/) and [UAE Federal Tax Authority](https://tax.gov.ae/). This guide is general information, not advice on your facts.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is an India-first holding structure?

The founders own an Indian private limited company, which is the head office and top of the group. The Indian company sets up a US C-Corp, a UAE company or both as wholly owned subsidiaries to sell, sign contracts and hire abroad. Investors come in at the Indian company.

### Can an Indian private limited company own a US or UAE company?

Yes. An Indian company can make overseas direct investment under the Overseas Investment Rules, 2022 through its authorised dealer bank. Under the automatic route its total financial commitment can go up to 400% of its net worth as per its last audited balance sheet, and the foreign company must be in a bona fide business.

### Do founders need to make ODI themselves in this structure?

No. The founders hold shares only in the Indian company. The overseas investment is made by the Indian company, so the individual ODI restrictions and the LRS limit do not come into it. That is one of the main reasons founders prefer this structure when they do not need a US parent.

### Are profits of the US or UAE subsidiary taxed in India?

Not while they stay in the subsidiary, as long as it is genuinely managed abroad. They are taxed in India when paid to the Indian parent as dividends, with credit for foreign tax under the tax treaty. If the subsidiary is really run from India, it can be treated as Indian-resident under the place of effective management test.

### What tax applies on dividends from the US subsidiary?

Under the India-US DTAA, US withholding tax on dividends is limited to 15% where the Indian company holds at least 10% of the voting stock. The dividend is then taxed in India in the parent's hands with credit for the US tax.

### Is a UAE subsidiary a tax-free company?

No. UAE corporate tax is 0% on taxable income up to AED 375,000 and 9% above that. A qualifying free zone person can get 0% on qualifying income only if it has real substance in the free zone and meets the other conditions. A UAE company that only books profits shifted from India also invites transfer pricing and POEM challenges in India.

### When should a startup choose a Delaware parent instead?

When US venture investors or accelerators make a Delaware parent a condition of investing. US funds usually want to invest at the top of the group, so an Indian holding company with a US subsidiary may not suit them. In that case look at a flip or the LLP triangle structure.

# DPT-3 for Startups: Why Director Loans Still Need a Return of Deposits

Published November 18, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- **DPT-3** is an annual return reporting deposits and also certain money received that is **not** a deposit, such as loans from directors. A startup with such loans outstanding on March 31 generally has to file it.
- **Due date: June 30** each year, reporting the position as on March 31. The FY 2025-26 return was due June 30, 2026; the FY 2026-27 return is due June 30, 2027.
- Money from a **director or relative of a director** is an exempted receipt only if the director gives a **written declaration** that it is not funded by borrowing or accepting loans or deposits from others.
- An **auditor certificate** is needed where the return reports actual deposits. A return that only reports exempted receipts does not need one.
- Late filing attracts additional MCA fees that grow with delay, plus a Rule 21 penalty. **Accepting a real deposit in breach of the rules** is far more serious (Section 76A).

Starting a company in India?

We incorporate your private limited company and run its first year of ROC compliance (INC-20A, first board meeting, auditor appointment, AOC-4 and MGT-7).

[Book a free startup call](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=startups)[See the startup package](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/startups#packages)

Founders are often surprised to hear from their CA that they must file a "return of deposits" when the company has never taken a deposit from the public. The reason is simple. The form is not only about deposits. It also asks the company to report money received that is exempt from the deposit definition, and a startup funded by director loans has exactly that.

## Who Has to File DPT-3

Every company other than a Government company that has an outstanding loan or receipt of money as on March 31, whether or not it is a deposit, is generally expected to file Form DPT-3. If nothing of this kind is outstanding on March 31, there is typically nothing to report. A startup that took an unsecured loan from a founder to cover its first year's costs is the standard example.

## Due Date

DPT-3 is annual and due by **June 30**, reporting the position as on the preceding March 31, unless MCA extends the date. If you missed the FY 2025-26 return, file now rather than waiting for the next cycle, because the additional fee keeps growing. Add the date to your [startup compliance calendar](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/startup-compliance-calendar-year-1-3).

## Deposit Versus Exempted Receipt

The Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014 define a deposit broadly as any receipt of money by way of deposit or loan, and then list what is excluded. For a small private company, the exclusions that matter most are:

- **Amount received from a director or a relative of a director**, provided the director furnishes a written declaration at the time of giving the money that it is not being given out of funds acquired by borrowing or accepting loans or deposits from others.
- **Bank and financial institution loans**, which are not deposits.
- **Share application money** received within the conditions of the Act, until it is allotted or refunded.
- **Advances for supply of goods or services**, if adjusted within the prescribed period.
- For a **private company**, money from members is allowed up to a limit linked to paid-up capital, free reserves and securities premium, subject to the conditions in the Rules. Check the current wording of the Rules before relying on this.

The catch is the declaration. Without it, a loan from a director is not automatically exempt, and the company has to treat it as a deposit and meet the deposit rules. Get the declaration in writing every time money comes in, and keep it with the company records. Related reading: [related party loans and Sections 185 and 186](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/related-party-loans-and-section-185-186-compliance).

## Auditor Certificate: When It Applies

If the return reports **actual deposits**, an auditor certificate is required. If it reports only exempted receipts such as declared director loans, an auditor certificate is not required, though the figures must still tie to the audited books and notes. Directors should be able to produce the declarations for each exempted receipt.

## Late Fee and Penalty

A late DPT-3 attracts an additional fee that rises in steps with the days of delay, so a return a few weeks late costs a small multiple of the normal fee and one many months late costs several times more. Rule 21 of the Deposit Rules also provides a penalty for failing to file, with a daily amount for continuing default. Reported figures vary across professional sources, so confirm the current amounts against the MCA fee schedule before filing.

Do not confuse a late filing with a deposit breach. Accepting a deposit that the Act does not permit, or failing to repay one on time, falls under Section 76A and carries heavy penalties for the company and officers. A company that has only filed late is in a far better position than one that took money it should not have.

## Practical Steps for a Startup

1. On March 31, list every loan or receipt outstanding: director loans, founder advances, shareholder loans, customer advances, bank loans.
2. For each, record the lender, amount and whether the exempt condition (such as the director declaration) is met.
3. Collect missing declarations before filing. Do not backdate them.
4. Match the figures to the audited balance sheet and the related-party note.
5. File DPT-3 by June 30 and keep the SRN with your records. See also our guide to [annual ROC filings](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/annual-roc-filing-aoc4-mgt7-dir3-kyc).

If you are raising money from friends and family or from angels, take advice before the money arrives. The classification can change whether it is a deposit, equity, or a convertible instrument, as covered in our post on [convertible notes versus equity](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/convertible-notes-vs-equity-fema-startups). Our [startup advisory](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/startups) team can structure it correctly.

**Official sources:** Sections 73, 74 and 76A of the Companies Act, 2013; Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, including Rules 16 and 21. See [Ministry of Corporate Affairs](https://www.mca.gov.in/).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do I need to file DPT-3 if my startup has only director loans?

Generally yes. DPT-3 also reports certain receipts that are not deposits, and a company with a director or unsecured loan outstanding on March 31 is expected to report it. If nothing is outstanding on March 31, there is typically nothing to report.

### What is the due date for DPT-3?

June 30 each year, reporting the position as on March 31, unless MCA extends it. The return for FY 2025-26 was due on June 30, 2026.

### When is a loan from a director not treated as a deposit?

When the director gives a written declaration, at the time of giving the money, that it is not out of funds acquired by borrowing or accepting loans or deposits from others. Without the declaration, the company may have to treat it as a deposit.

### Is an auditor certificate required for DPT-3?

It is required where the return reports actual deposits. A return reporting only exempted receipts, such as declared director loans, does not need the certificate.

### What happens if DPT-3 is filed late?

An additional MCA fee applies and increases with the delay, and Rule 21 of the Deposit Rules provides a penalty for failure to file. Confirm current amounts on the MCA fee schedule. This is separate from the much heavier Section 76A penalties for breaching the deposit rules.

### Are bank loans and share application money reported in DPT-3?

Bank loans and properly held share application money are not deposits. Whether they appear in the exempted receipts part of the form depends on the form instructions, so check them with your CA while preparing the return.

US Cross-Border

# Form 5472 Penalty: How to Fix Missed Filings for Your Foreign-Owned US LLC

Published November 18, 2026Updated November 18, 2026[CA Mehul Agrawal](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/about#mehul-agrawal)Agrawal Khandelwal & Associates LLP

TL;DR

- The IRS instructions state a USD 25,000 penalty for failing to file Form 5472 on time, per form and per year.
- Capital contributions and distributions between you and the LLC are reportable, so a no-income LLC can still owe the filing.
- Due April 15, or October 15 with Form 7004. A foreign-owned US disregarded entity files by fax or mail with the pro forma Form 1120, not electronically.
- If you missed years, reconstruct the transactions and file each year with a reasonable cause statement, ideally before the IRS writes to you.
- Relief is not guaranteed. Reasonable cause needs real facts; first-time abatement for Form 5472 is disputed, so do not count on it.

Running a US LLC or C-Corp from India?

Our team prepares your US filings and our US partner reviews and files them, while we keep your Indian side (ITR, FEMA, transfer pricing) in step.

[Book a US compliance call](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/consult?topic=us-cross-border)[See US packages](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/us-cross-border#packages)

The most expensive mistake we see in foreign-owned US LLCs is not wrong tax. It is a missing form. A single-member LLC with no income can owe nothing in tax and still face a USD 25,000 penalty for not filing Form 5472. If you are an Indian resident who owns a US LLC, this guide covers the penalty, how to catch up on missed years and what relief may be available. For the difference between Forms 5471, 5472 and 8858, see our [form comparison guide](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/form-5471-5472-8858-foreign-owned-us-entity); this post stays on penalties and catch-up.

## The Penalty in Plain Numbers

The IRS instructions for Form 5472 state a penalty of **USD 25,000** for failing to file the form on time and in the required manner, or to keep the required records. Three points matter:

- It is charged **per form, per year**. Three missed years means three penalties.
- A substantially incomplete Form 5472 is treated as a failure to file.
- If the failure continues more than 90 days after the IRS notifies you, an additional USD 25,000 applies for each related party, for each 30-day period (or part of one) after the 90 days. The instructions also mention criminal penalties in serious cases.

## What Must Be Reported

For a foreign-owned disregarded entity, the form reports transactions with the foreign owner and other related parties. Reportable items include money in and out, such as **capital contributions and distributions**, loans, payments for services, rent or royalties, and formation, dissolution or acquisition events. Monetary transactions go in Part IV, other owner transactions in Part V (a statement describing contributions, distributions and similar items), and non-monetary or below-market transactions in Part VI. A founder who simply funded the LLC bank account and later withdrew money has reportable transactions, even if the LLC earned nothing.

## Due Dates and How to File

Form 5472 is attached to a pro forma Form 1120 and is due with the entity's return. For a calendar-year LLC that is **April 15**, or **October 15** if Form 7004 is filed by April 15. Per the IRS instructions, a foreign-owned US disregarded entity cannot file electronically. Write "Foreign-owned U.S. DE" across the top of the pro forma Form 1120 and either fax it (300 DPI or higher) to the IRS number given in the Form 5472 instructions or mail it to the Ogden, Utah PIN Unit address given there. Do not use the general Form 1120 mailing address. Form 7004 goes to the same fax number or address, not the normal 7004 address. Check the current instructions for the exact details before sending.

## Catching Up on Missed Years

1. **List every year since formation** and every transaction with you as the owner: money put in, money taken out, loans, payments to you.
2. **Check whether the IRS has already written to you.** The IRS delinquent international information return procedures apply only to taxpayers not under examination and not already contacted about the delinquent returns. The IRS page does not name Form 5472, so confirm with a professional that the route fits your facts.
3. **Prepare each missing year's pro forma Form 1120 and Form 5472** with a reasonable cause statement attached, and file them through the fax or mail route above.
4. **Respond promptly if a penalty notice arrives.** The 90-day clock for additional penalties starts from the IRS notification, so do not let a letter sit.

Filing late does not by itself cancel the penalty. The IRS page notes that penalties may still be assessed without considering the attached reasonable cause statement, and you may need to respond to the IRS and resubmit your explanation.

## Penalty Relief: What We Can and Cannot Promise

The law allows relief where the failure was due to reasonable cause and not willful neglect, and practitioners argue it on documented facts. Not knowing about the rule, or relying on someone to file for you, is commonly reported to be a weak ground by itself, so a statement needs real facts. First-time abatement is different: practitioner sources disagree on whether it applies to Form 5472 penalties, and some say it reaches them only where the related Form 1120 is abated. We have not confirmed the position in the Internal Revenue Manual, so treat it as uncertain and not as a plan. No firm can guarantee a waiver.

## Prevent It From Happening Again

Put the filing in your calendar every year, keep a ledger of every owner contribution and withdrawal, and keep the US bookkeeping current so the Part IV and V figures are ready. Our team prepares the filing and a US partner reviews and files it. See our [US LLC compliance calendar](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/us-llc-annual-compliance-calendar-non-resident) for the full list, [US LLC vs C-Corp](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/blog/us-llc-vs-c-corp-indian-founders) if you are reconsidering the structure, and our [US cross-border advisory](https://agrawalkhandelwal.com/us-cross-border) page for how we work.
